source_scope: 34 non-archived TheAlgorithms algorithm repositories. Portable-language source paths can supply benchmark implementations; AArch64 Assembly paths are included only as discovery references.
matching_method: Normalize each source filename stem (including camelCase to snake_case); Project Euler solN files include their problem number. Identical normalized stems are candidate matches only and have not been checked for equivalent behavior. Candidates may declare benchmark_name when a numeric or otherwise non-descriptive source stem needs an alphabetic algorithm folder, and additional_benchmark_names when one source candidate contains multiple distinct benchmarkable algorithms.
excluded_paths: Tests, examples, benchmarks, documentation, scripts, build output, and vendor directories are omitted.

source_repositories.usage: discovery reference only; architecture-specific assembly is not a portable benchmark implementation

candidates.review_notes: The pinned Dart source uses the direct recursive include-or-exclude recurrence without memoization. It is kept distinct from the bottom-up tabulation benchmark so their runtime and call-stack behavior can be compared. The shared contract bounds the item count to 16 to keep the exponential recurrence practical and defines malformed inputs explicitly.

The pinned Jupyter notebook is an end-to-end Keras IMDB sentiment-classification workflow: it loads a remote dataset, trains a neural network, evaluates it, and plots results. It is not a standalone deterministic algorithm with a bounded callable input/output contract, so it is excluded from the benchmark catalog.

The pinned C++ source fills a bottom-up 0/1 knapsack table with the same item/capacity recurrence as the canonical tabulation candidate. This filename is retained as an alias to share one workload and contract.

The pinned C LeetCode source solves the Two Sum problem with nested scans under the source problem's single-solution assumption. It overwrites the result for each matching pair, so multiple matches select the last pair in scan order, and a no-solution input returns a zero-filled pair. The shared benchmark defines an explicit no-pair sentinel and a deterministic earliest-pair rule; this numeric filename is reviewed as an alias of that standardized Two Sum contract.

The pinned C LeetCode source performs recursive full-string matching with '.' for one character and '*' for zero or more repetitions of its preceding atom. It has the same matching semantics as the Python recursive_match implementation and aliases that contract.

The pinned C LeetCode 1008 source recursively partitions a valid BST preorder at each root and constructs left and right subtrees. The shared contract validates unique signed 32-bit keys, bounds the input to 15 nodes, and emits an explicit preorder tree serialization with null markers.

The pinned C LeetCode 1009 source uses ceil(log2(n)) to form a low-bit mask and returns ~n masked to that width; this produces the standard significant-bit complement, including for exact powers of two. C LeetCode 476 builds the equivalent mask by finding the most significant bit. The shared benchmark handles zero explicitly and follows the 1009 constraint 0 <= n < 1,000,000,000, keeping the C signed-shift behavior defined.

The pinned C LeetCode 101 source recursively compares mirrored node pairs, matching the canonical symmetric_tree contract. An adapter represents the source pointer tree as the package indexed triplet table.

The pinned C LeetCode source scans the remaining linked list from each node and records the first strictly greater value, defaulting to zero when no later node qualifies. This is an O(n^2) forward-scan algorithm. The shared contract bounds the list to 4,096 positive signed 32-bit values and serializes one result per node as little-endian bytes.

The pinned C LeetCode source recursively tracks the minimum and maximum value on each root-to-node path and updates the maximum absolute difference. The shared benchmark uses a bounded indexed-tree contract and portable implementations in all nine target languages.

The pinned C LeetCode source returns zero for a null tree and otherwise recursively returns one plus the larger child depth. The shared contract uses an indexed binary tree and portable recursive implementations in all nine target languages.

The pinned C LeetCode 108 implementation recursively selects the midpoint of the sorted input, allocates that key, and builds left and right subtrees; an empty input returns a null tree. The shared contract names the algorithm sorted_array_to_bst, requires strictly increasing signed 32-bit keys, uses the lower median for even ranges, and serializes the tree in preorder with null markers.

The pinned C LeetCode 1089 source copies the fixed-length array, then writes each original value and a second zero slot when needed; the output remains the original length. The shared contract accepts values 0 through 1,000, validates a bounded array, and serializes the transformed fixed-length result.

The pinned C LeetCode 109 source recursively uses slow and fast linked-list pointers to select each subtree root; this walk chooses the upper middle for even-sized sublists. The shared contract supplies the sorted list values as an array, accepts nondecreasing signed 32-bit sequences, and serializes the balanced tree in preorder.

The pinned C LeetCode 11 source implements the two-pointer maximum-container-area algorithm. The shared contract accepts nonnegative signed 32-bit heights and returns the maximum area as signed 64-bit; invalid heights and lengths are rejected.

The pinned C LeetCode source computes each node's left and right heights, then recursively checks both child subtrees; null trees are balanced. The benchmark preserves that repeated-height recursive approach under a bounded indexed-tree contract in all nine target languages.

The pinned C LeetCode 112 function recursively subtracts each node value from the requested sum and succeeds only at a leaf. The shared contract packs an indexed binary tree with a signed 64-bit target, validates that every node is reachable exactly once from root index 0, and returns whether any root-to-leaf path matches.
The pinned C LeetCode implementation uses T(0)=0, T(1)=1, T(2)=1 and the same nth-term recurrence as the canonical tribonacci benchmark.

The pinned C LeetCode 1147 candidate recursively peels matching prefix and suffix chunks and counts a remaining center chunk. The shared contract accepts 0 to 128 ASCII byte values in 1..127 and returns the maximum number of chunks; invalid input returns -1.
The pinned C LeetCode 118 source generates the first numRows rows of Pascal’s triangle, matching the canonical coefficient sequence.

The pinned C LeetCode 1184 function sums the distances on the two arcs between the selected stops and returns the smaller sum. The shared contract packs endpoint indices before 1 to 64 nonnegative distances bounded at 1,000,000.

The pinned C LeetCode 1189 candidate counts lowercase ASCII letters and returns the minimum of b, a, l/2, o/2, and n. The shared contract accepts 0 to 256 lowercase ASCII byte values and returns -1 for invalid input.

The pinned C LeetCode 119 source builds the requested zero-based Pascal-triangle row in place, updating interior coefficients from right to left. The shared contract bounds the row index to 0 through 33, matching its 32-bit coefficient domain, and serializes coefficients as little-endian unsigned 32-bit values.
The pinned C LeetCode filename 12 implements integer-to-Roman conversion for the standard 1 through 3,999 range. It aliases the descriptive integer_to_roman benchmark.

The pinned C LeetCode 1207 candidate sorts bounded occurrence counts and rejects duplicate positive frequencies. The shared contract accepts 0 to 1,000 values in -1,000..1,000; invalid input returns -1.

The pinned C LeetCode source computes the maximum subarray sum over adjacent price differences with Kadane's algorithm. This is equivalent to the single-buy/single-sell maximum-profit contract and aliases the shared stock benchmark.

The pinned C source implements the same recursive maximum-path-sum recurrence as the Python candidate binary_tree_maximum_path_sum. Its LOWER_BOUND declaration is missing a semicolon; the benchmark ports implement the evident intended algorithm.

The pinned C LeetCode 125 source uses inward-moving indices, skips non-alphanumeric characters, and compares ASCII letters without case sensitivity. The shared contract makes classification explicitly ASCII and uses a length-prefixed sequence of code points.

The pinned C LeetCode 1283 candidate binary-searches the least divisor whose rounded quotient sum meets the threshold. The shared contract packs the threshold before 1 to 256 positive values bounded at 1,000,000; thresholds below the item count return -1.

The pinned C LeetCode 13 source converts standard Roman symbols using additive values and subtracts I, X, or C before their valid higher pairs. It aliases the canonical Roman decoder under its uppercase 1 through 3,999 contract.
The pinned C LeetCode source XORs all signed 32-bit values, which returns the single value when every other value occurs twice. It aliases the shared single_number XOR contract.

The pinned C LeetCode filename 14 contains findMaxConsecutiveOnes, which counts contiguous nonzero values. On the standardized binary domain this is the maximum-consecutive-ones algorithm, so candidate 14 aliases max_consecutive_ones.

The pinned C LeetCode 141 source uses Floyd’s tortoise and hare pointers to report whether the list reachable from the head contains a cycle. The portable contract represents each next pointer as a signed node index, uses -1 for null and node 0 as the head, and returns 1 for a cycle, 0 for an acyclic path, or -1 for malformed input.

The pinned C LeetCode 142 source first finds a Floyd tortoise-and-hare meeting point, then advances one pointer from the head and one from the meeting point to locate the cycle entry. The portable contract uses successor indices with -1 for null and node 0 as the head, returning the zero-based entry index, -1 for an acyclic path, or -2 for malformed input.
The pinned C LeetCode 1524 candidate counts subarrays with odd sums using prefix parities. The shared contract accepts 0 to 100,000 signed 32-bit values and returns the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

The pinned C LeetCode 153 source compares the midpoint with the high endpoint and narrows the search interval to the minimum. The shared contract preserves the source assumption of a nonempty rotation of a strictly increasing array and bounds the input to 256 signed 64-bit values.

The pinned C LeetCode 16 source sorts the values and uses a two-pointer scan for the closest three-value sum. Its qsort mutates the input and its int difference calculation can overflow outside the original narrow problem bounds. The shared contract copies and heapsorts signed 32-bit values, widens sums and distance calculations to signed 64-bit, defines lower-sum tie resolution, and bounds the item count to 512.

The pinned C LeetCode 160 source advances two pointers and switches each to the other list head after reaching the end, returning the shared node pointer or null. The shared contract encodes pointer identity as nonnegative node IDs in two acyclic lists with aligned shared suffixes; nine portable ports preserve the O(m+n) head-switching traversal.

The pinned C LeetCode 1653 candidate uses a linear two-state dynamic program to minimize deletions that leave all a characters before all b characters. The shared contract packs a as 0 and b as 1, accepts up to 256 symbols, and returns -1 for invalid symbols or excess length.

The pinned C LeetCode 1657 candidate checks equal lowercase character sets and compares sorted occurrence counts. The shared contract packs two strings, each up to 256 lowercase ASCII bytes, after their lengths.
The pinned C LeetCode 169 source uses Boyer-Moore cancellation for the strict majority candidate. It matches the C-Sharp canonical algorithm; this numeric filename is recorded as an alias.

The pinned C LeetCode 1695 candidate uses a last-occurrence sliding window to maximize the sum of a contiguous subarray with distinct values. The shared contract accepts 0 to 256 values in 1..10,000 and returns -1 for invalid values or excess length.
The pinned C LeetCode 17 source emits the standard 2–9 keypad Cartesian product in the same order as the canonical phone-letter-combinations benchmark.
The pinned C LeetCode 1704 candidate counts vowels in equal string halves. The shared contract accepts even-length ASCII letter arrays up to 256 bytes and returns -1 for odd lengths or invalid bytes.

The pinned C LeetCode 173 source counts BST nodes, recursively materializes an in-order values array, then implements next by advancing an index and hasNext by checking whether a value remains. The shared indexed-tree contract returns an order-sensitive checksum for the full iterator trace; nine portable ports preserve eager materialization and sequential consumption.

The pinned C LeetCode 1752 candidate detects at most one descending adjacent pair in the circular array. The shared contract accepts 0 to 256 signed 32-bit values and returns -1 for invalid values or excess length.

The pinned C LeetCode 1769 candidate computes all per-box move distances in two linear passes. The shared contract accepts 0 to 256 binary occupancy values and serializes one unsigned 16-bit little-endian move count per box; invalid values, excess length, and insufficient capacity have explicit results.

The pinned C LeetCode 1833 candidate sorts positive bar costs, then greedily buys the cheapest bars while the budget allows. The shared contract packs a budget followed by up to 256 costs, with explicit ranges and invalid-input behavior.

The pinned C LeetCode 1838 candidate sorts values and uses a sliding window with prefix sums to find the largest group that can be raised to one value within budget. The shared contract packs budget and up to 256 values into one array and defines portable bounds and invalid-input behavior.

The pinned C LeetCode 189 source performs k right rotations by moving the last array value to index zero and shifting all preceding values one place on each pass. The shared contract defines signed 32-bit values, k from 0 through 1,024, and separate little-endian output; nine portable ports preserve the repeated-shift method.

The pinned C LeetCode 19 source counts nodes, walks to the predecessor of the one-based position from the tail, unlinks that node, and returns the updated head. It assumes the position is valid; this candidate aliases the Python remove_nth_node_from_end_of_list candidate under the shared bounded-list contract.

C LeetCode 190 explicitly reverses all 32 positions of an unsigned word, matching the Java, Python, and Rust reverse_bits sources. It is recorded as an alias of the shared fixed-width bit-reversal contract.

The pinned C LeetCode 191 source counts set bits across an unsigned 32-bit value. The C++ count_of_set_bits and JavaScript BinaryCountSetBits sources have the same result on this shared domain. The benchmark accepts the value through a signed 64-bit ABI, counts valid values from 0 through 2^32-1, and returns -1 outside that range.

Both pinned R files implement bottom-up 0/1 knapsack dynamic programming: one exposes a full table with item backtracking and a descending one-row space-optimized form, and the other also includes the same full-table and optimized recurrence. Their maximum-value result matches the shared 0/1 tabulation benchmark, so this candidate is an alias rather than a new algorithm.

The pinned C LeetCode 2 source adds the two least-significant-first digit lists node by node, propagates carry, and allocates one result node per processed digit including a final carry. The shared byte-output contract encodes both lists in one packed input and serializes result digits least-significant first.

The pinned C LeetCode 20 source uses a stack for matching parentheses, square brackets, and braces. Its stack semantics match the Java ValidParentheses candidate; this numeric filename is recorded as an alias of valid_parentheses.

The pinned C LeetCode 201 source clears the least significant set bit of the upper endpoint with n &= n - 1 until it equals the lower endpoint. The shared contract accepts inclusive nonnegative ranges through INT32_MAX and returns -1 for invalid bounds. Nine portable ports preserve the endpoint bit-clearing algorithm.

The pinned C LeetCode 2024 source runs a sliding window for each answer character, T and F, allowing at most k changes to the other character. The shared contract packs k followed by 0/1 answer values, limits sequences to 1,024 entries, and returns the longest run for either target.

The pinned C LeetCode 203 source recursively removes every node matching the target and returns the possibly changed head. The shared benchmark builds an index-based link chain, recursively rewrites retained-node links, and serializes surviving signed 32-bit values in list order.

The pinned AArch64 source is an interactive Linux terminal game rather than a standalone algorithm entry point. It includes architecture-specific termios, signal, poll, keyboard, random tile-spawn, display, and replay code. Extracting only its directional move kernels would be a new subalgorithm contract and would not cover this full program candidate, so it is excluded from the portable benchmark inventory.

The pinned C LeetCode 206 source iteratively reverses a singly linked list by redirecting each next pointer to the previous node. The linked-list operation trace now includes opcode 7 for this in-place reversal; all nine ports pass the extended trace oracle.

The pinned C LeetCode 2095 source counts the list, then uses fast and slow pointers plus the node-count parity to unlink the floor(n / 2)-indexed node; empty and singleton lists return an empty list. The shared indexed-link benchmark preserves the count pass, fast/slow traversal, unlink, and ordered signed 32-bit serialization.

The pinned C LeetCode 21 file contains iterative and recursive definitions of the same function; the benchmark selects its iterative linear two-pointer merge. The shared contract bounds both inputs to a combined 1,024 signed 32-bit values, validates sorted order, and serializes the merged ascending result.

The pinned C LeetCode 2125 source counts devices in each row, skips empty rows without resetting the previous nonempty count, and adds the product for every adjacent pair of nonempty rows. No existing benchmark has this grid-counting contract. The nine portable ports use a fixed-width row-major ASCII encoding.

The pinned C LeetCode 2130 source first copies linked-list values into an array, then scans mirrored indices in the first half and returns the largest pair sum. The contract preserves the source problem’s even list length and positive values from 1 through 100,000. No existing benchmark covers maximum mirrored-pair sums.

The pinned C LeetCode 215 source sorts the complete array in descending order with qsort and returns rank k - 1. This full-sort strategy is distinct from the Python candidate kth_largest_element, which uses iterative Lomuto quickselect, and is benchmarked separately.

The pinned C LeetCode 217 source sorts the integer array and scans adjacent values. The shared contract accepts up to 1,024 signed 32-bit integers and returns 1 for a repeated value, 0 otherwise, or -1 for invalid values or lengths. Each port sorts a private copy with portable heapsort.

The pinned C LeetCode 2222 source counts 010 and 101 subsequences with two linear passes. The shared contract represents the binary string as ASCII values, bounds its length to 4096, and the nine portable ports count both patterns in O(n) time and O(1) space.

The pinned C LeetCode 223 source computes the sum of two rectangle areas minus their positive-area intersection. The shared contract uses eight bounded signed coordinates and valid nonempty rectangles. The nine portable ports use integer clipping and return a signed 64-bit union area in O(1) time and space.

The pinned C LeetCode 2256 source sums the array, then scans all prefixes and compares truncated integer averages for the prefix and remaining suffix; a missing suffix average is zero. The shared contract bounds nonnegative values to 0..100000 and length to 100000, preserving integer division and first-index tie behavior. All nine ports use two linear scans and constant auxiliary space.

The pinned C LeetCode 226 source recursively swaps each node’s left and right links. The shared indexed-tree contract serializes the mirrored node table in little-endian signed 64-bit triplets so all nine portable implementations can be compared exactly.

The pinned C LeetCode 2270 source sums the array, then scans each valid prefix split and counts positions where the left sum is at least the remaining right sum. The shared contract bounds signed values to -100000..100000 and length to 2..100000; all nine portable ports use 64-bit sums and two linear scans with constant auxiliary space.

The pinned C LeetCode 2279 source computes each bag’s remaining capacity from its capacity and current rocks, sorts those deficits, then greedily spends additional rocks on the smallest deficits first. The shared packed contract preserves the budget, bag count, capacities, and rocks; it bounds the bag count to 8191 so the identical fixed work array fits below C3’s 64 KiB stack-object limit. All nine ports compute deficits, heap-sort them, and scan the affordable prefix.

The pinned C LeetCode 230 source performs recursive inorder DFS, decrements k at each node, and returns as soon as the rank reaches zero. The benchmark preserves this early exit over unique-value BSTs, extends the node-value contract to include zero as allowed by LeetCode, and limits trees to 1,023 nodes for the portable indexed-tree ABI. All nine ports pass the independent inorder oracle.

The pinned C LeetCode 2304 source uses row-by-row dynamic programming: for each next column it minimizes the prior path cost plus the current grid value and the value-indexed move cost, then adds the final-row cell value. The shared packed contract uses rectangular grids and a complete move-cost table, with each dimension bounded to 32. All nine ports keep two column-sized DP rows and run in O(rows * columns^2) time.
The pinned C LeetCode source checks positivity and applies the standard n & (n - 1) power-of-two predicate, matching the existing signed 64-bit benchmark semantics on the source's integer domain.

The pinned C LeetCode 234 source uses slow/fast pointers, reverses the second half of the linked list, and compares values. The shared ABI represents the values in order as a read-only array, so the benchmark compares from both ends with O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space while preserving the palindrome result. The contract accepts up to 100,000 digits in 0..9, extends empty input as a palindrome, and returns -1 for invalid inputs. All nine ports passed 10,656 oracle arrays and 11 workload cases.

The pinned C LeetCode 236 source builds root-to-target paths for p and q, then returns the last node in their longest common prefix. The shared indexed-tree contract returns the ancestor table index and requires distinct, uniquely valued targets. All nine ports pass 23,424 valid and malformed packed-tree cases against an independent parent-set oracle and record all six workload cases; see build/lowest_common_ancestor/verification.json.

The pinned C LeetCode 24 source recursively rewires adjacent linked-list nodes and leaves an unpaired final node in place. The shared bounded array contract serializes the same pairwise order transformation as signed 32-bit values.

The pinned C LeetCode 242 source counts lowercase ASCII letters in each input string and compares the two 26-entry frequency tables. The shared packed-array contract validates lowercase ASCII values, string lengths through 1,024, and an exact packed length; it returns 1 for matching frequencies, 0 otherwise, and -1 for malformed input.

The pinned C LeetCode 2482 source counts ones in each row and column, but uses the opposite dimension when deriving zero counts on rectangular matrices. The benchmark follows the stated formula onesRow[r] + onesColumn[c] - zerosRow[r] - zerosColumn[c], accepts matrices up to 100,000 cells, and serializes signed 32-bit little-endian results. All nine portable ports run in O(rows * columns) time and reuse the output buffer for row/column counts instead of using architecture-specific optimizations.

The pinned C LeetCode 2501 source marks values present in a set, memoizes square-chain lengths, and takes the maximum chain with at least two values. The shared contract accepts 2 through 100,000 values in 2..100,000 and uses a 400,004-byte caller workspace for portable presence and memo states, avoiding large stack arrays and per-language allocation differences. All nine ports use the same O(n + maxValue) recurrence and leave input unchanged.

The pinned C LeetCode 26 source uses a write index to compact an ascending array in place and returns the unique-prefix length. The shared bounded contract serializes that prefix as signed 32-bit values and leaves the input buffer unchanged.

The pinned C LeetCode 268 source subtracts the observed array sum from the arithmetic-series sum for 0 through n. The shared contract validates distinct inputs in [0,n], permits the empty array, and returns its unique missing value.

The pinned C LeetCode 27 source uses a write index to remove every matching target in place and returns the survivor count. The shared contract accepts a target followed by signed 32-bit values and serializes stable survivors to a separate output buffer.

The pinned C LeetCode 274 source sorts citations in place and scans from largest to smallest. The shared array-scalar ABI is read-only, so the benchmark preserves the H-index definition with an upper-midpoint binary search over h and a count of citations >= h. The contract accepts 0 through 5,000 values in 0..1,000, returns 0 for empty input, and returns -1 for invalid input. All nine ports use O(n log(min(n, 1000))) time, O(1) auxiliary space, and do not mutate input.

The pinned C LeetCode 278 source performs lower-bound binary search using an external isBadVersion API. The benchmark represents that monotone predicate with a first_bad input and tests middle >= first_bad, preserving the O(log n) algorithm and avoiding an external dependency. The shared contract supports version counts through 2^31-1, validates the predicate boundary, and uses an overflow-safe midpoint. All nine portable ports passed 9,105 oracle pairs and 15 workload cases.

The pinned C LeetCode 28 file defines strStr twice: an initial direct character scan with O(mn) worst-case work, followed by a KMP implementation with O(m+n) work. The KMP implementation aliases the existing KMP benchmark, and the direct scan is recorded separately as str_str_brute_force.

The pinned C LeetCode 283 source stably compacts nonzero values toward the front, then fills the remaining positions with zero. The shared contract keeps the input read-only to the caller and returns the same-length result in a separate little-endian signed 32-bit buffer.

The pinned C LeetCode 287 source sorts the input and scans adjacent values, which mutates the array and misses the problem's linear-time, constant-space follow-up. The benchmark follows the official contract with Floyd's cycle-entry algorithm, accepts up to 100,000 values plus the repeated entry, and leaves input unchanged. All nine ports passed 17,733 exhaustive/randomized/frequency-oracle arrays and 12 workload cases, including the maximum 100,001-value input.

The pinned C LeetCode 29 source doubles the divisor to subtract large multiples while keeping working values nonpositive. The shared contract widens signed 32-bit values, truncates toward zero, and saturates the quotient to the signed 32-bit range.

The pinned C LeetCode 3 source contains an O(n) last-seen-index implementation and a separate brute-force duplicate definition; the O(n) implementation returns the longest substring length. It is reviewed as a LeetCode-number alias of the alphabetically named benchmark.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 32 implementation. It uses a memoized endpoint recurrence to find the longest well-formed contiguous parenthesis substring. The shared contract encodes parentheses as ASCII values in a bounded signed 64-bit array; the nine portable ports evaluate the recurrence bottom-up to avoid recursion-depth dependence.

The pinned C LeetCode 344 source reverses a char array in place by swapping its left and right endpoints while moving inward. The shared byte-array contract validates values 0..255 and adapts mutation to a separate output buffer while preserving the same two-pointer swaps.

The pinned C LeetCode 35 file contains two conflicting definitions of searchInsert. The first, iterative definition performs binary search; the benchmark follows it for strictly increasing signed 32-bit arrays and returns the lower-bound insertion index.
The pinned C LeetCode 367 source reports whether a nonnegative integer is a perfect square; its loop implementation shares the canonical exact square predicate.

The pinned C LeetCode 37 source intends row, column, and 3x3-box occupancy tracking with recursive backtracking, but it recurses before writing the trial digit into the board, so it revisits the same blank. The nine ports implement the intended row-major search with the digit placed before recursion and removed after a failed branch. The independent verifier confirms unique solutions and checks all nine ports.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 38 implementation. It starts with the term "1" and repeatedly emits each run length followed by its digit. The shared contract uses a bounded one-based index of 1 through 19 so all terms fit the portable 256-byte scalar-output ABI, and defines invalid-index and output-capacity behavior.

The pinned C LeetCode 387 source counts byte frequencies and returns the first unique character index. The shared contract uses the problem domain of lowercase ASCII letters, represented as integer byte values.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 389 implementation. It sums the character codes in both lowercase strings and returns target sum minus source sum; correctness relies on the target being a permutation with one extra character. The shared contract packs both explicit lengths and byte arrays into the scalar-array ABI, then uses the same sum method in nine portable ports.

The pinned Ruby source generates the Collatz trajectory beginning with the input and ending at 1, then formats it as text. The shared collatz_sequence contract represents those same values as portable little-endian integers for positive bounded inputs.

The pinned TheAlgorithms/Ruby source sorts a copy, skips duplicate first values, and uses a two-pointer search to enumerate unique zero-sum triplets. The nine target-language ports preserve that O(n^2) search and input immutability, with a portable heap sort and explicit little-endian triplet encoding. The local input bound is 257 (rather than LeetCode’s 3,000) so the conservative maximum output fits the existing byte-output ABI. All nine ports passed 4,175 oracle inputs and 12 workload records.

The pinned C LeetCode 4 source merges two already sorted arrays before selecting the median. This is algorithmically distinct from the one-array median benchmark, which insertion-sorts a single unsorted array. The cross-language contract packs two sorted signed-32-bit arrays and returns twice their exact statistical median.

The pinned C LeetCode source returns the sum of values at leaf nodes that are left children, recursively traversing both subtrees. The shared contract uses a bounded indexed tree and signed values in [-1000, 1000], with portable recursive ports in all nine target languages.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 42 implementation. It computes suffix maximum heights and a running prefix maximum, then sums trapped water, matching trapped_rainwater. Its source assumes a nonempty array; the shared benchmark contract defines empty input as zero and handles it safely.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 434 source. It counts transitions from ASCII space to non-space, treating only space as a delimiter. The shared contract uses an explicit-length nonzero ASCII byte array; all nine portable ports preserve the transition-count algorithm.

The pinned C LeetCode 442 source sorts the input, then scans adjacent values and emits each duplicate once; the problem contract guarantees each value appears at most twice. The shared benchmark returns those values in ascending order, encodes them as little-endian signed 32-bit values, and defines bounded input and output-capacity behavior. All nine ports passed 32,482 oracle inputs and recorded 12 workload cases.

The pinned C LeetCode 45 source explores reachable array indices in breadth-first layers, deduplicating enqueued positions with a visited array, and returns the first layer reaching the last index. The portable benchmark preserves BFS using one FIFO queue, visited flags, and per-index distances.

The pinned C LeetCode 461 source counts differing bits of two nonnegative signed 32-bit values. On this domain, zero-extending each value to the shared unsigned 64-bit hamming_distance contract preserves the result.
The pinned C LeetCode 476 source constructs a mask through the most significant input bit and returns the same significant-bit complement as candidate 1009.
The pinned C LeetCode 485 source counts contiguous ones in a binary array. Its shared binary-input contract is the same as max_consecutive_ones, so this candidate is an alias.

The pinned TheAlgorithms/C LeetCode 5 source describes center expansion for odd and even palindromes, but allocates only sizeof(pointer) bytes for its result. The benchmark preserves the O(n^2) center-expansion algorithm with caller-provided output storage. Its contract follows the official 1-to-1,000 ASCII alphanumeric input domain, returns the leftmost longest substring on ties, and uses -1/-2 for invalid input/insufficient capacity. All nine portable ports are checked against an independent interval dynamic-programming oracle.

The pinned C LeetCode 50 source computes powers by recursive repeated squaring and reciprocates negative exponents, with a special case for INT32_MIN. The nine ports preserve the repeated-squaring operation order under the shared binary64 base and signed 32-bit exponent contract.
The pinned C LeetCode 509 source computes the zero-based Fibonacci value with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1.

Inspected both detectCapitalUse definitions in the pinned C LeetCode 520 source. The first counts uppercase letters in O(n); the second invokes an all-uppercase scan for every uppercase byte after the first, giving O(n^2) worst-case work. The original file repeats the function definition, so each approach is cataloged separately with matching semantics and portable nine-language ports.

The pinned C LeetCode 53 source uses Kadane's recurrence and matches the maximum_subarray objective on nonempty arrays. Limit length to 1..1024 and each value to [-2097152,2097151], ensuring every contiguous sum fits the source signed C int and avoiding undefined overflow. The package's wider value domain is outside this source alias.

The pinned C LeetCode 540 source uses binary search on pair alignment in a sorted array where one value occurs once and all others occur twice. The shared contract preserves this precondition and returns the unique value.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 561 implementation. It sorts the input with qsort and sums every even-positioned value. The shared contract bounds values to signed 32-bit integers and requires an even length; nine portable ports use the same in-place heapsort procedure on a local copy.

The pinned C LeetCode 567 source maintains pattern-versus-window letter-count differences and a mismatch count while sliding across the text. The pinned JavaScript PermutationinString source also compares 26-letter frequency windows. The shared contract packs lowercase ASCII strings, limits each to 1,024 characters, and returns whether a permutation occurs as a contiguous substring; all nine ports use a fixed 26-entry table and portable integer operations.

Inspected the pinned C LeetCode 6 implementation. It emits the first and last rows with a fixed 2*(rows-1) gap and alternates complementary gaps for interior rows. The target and alphabet are printable ASCII and bounded to 8 target bytes and 32 genes; all nine portable implementations passed the shared deterministic oracle and workload.

The pinned C# sorter uses insertion sort on 32-element runs, then stable bottom-up merges at doubling run widths. Its comparison and tie behavior match the existing tim_sort contract, so the source candidate aliases that benchmark instead of duplicating its workload.

The pinned Python and Ruby sources calculate binary OR for two bounded nonnegative integers and format the result with a `0b` prefix and width determined by the operands. The contract preserves that byte output and rejects malformed or out-of-range inputs.

The pinned C# source is an infinite prime-characteristic sequence: at one-based index i, emit 1 iff i is prime and 0 otherwise. They alias bipartite_graph_dfs for valid bounded undirected graphs. The benchmark maps only the Boolean decision and bounds all neighbor IDs to the declared vertex list.

The pinned Java DFS starts from every uncolored vertex, covering disconnected components. The shared bounded contract accepts n=1..64 and up to 256 undirected edges; repeated edges do not change the result, while self-loops make the graph non-bipartite.

The pinned Rust source exposes both Kuhn's DFS augmenting-path matcher and Hopcroft–Karp's layered matcher. Preserve them as separate benchmarks under one packed bipartite graph contract: zero-based partition vertices, up to 64 vertices per side, up to 4096 edge records, duplicate edges accepted, and maximum cardinality as the scalar result. Malformed inputs return -1.

The pinned Python and MATLAB sources use interval bisection. Their endpoint and stopping checks differ (Python interval width; MATLAB residual), so this candidate aliases the shared bisection method under its normalized bracket/tolerance contract.

The pinned Python source bisects the fixed equation `10 - x*x` with a 0.01 interval-width threshold. The package preserves the initial `c=a` behavior for brackets already narrower than the threshold, returns an unscaled binary64 root estimate, and rejects invalid or unbracketed intervals.

The pinned C and C++ cubic demos are normalized as bounded bisection root finding, with a selector for each cubic and a rounded micro-root result. This is distinct from the existing square-root binary-search benchmark.

The pinned C# BitArray class exposes zero/one counts, even/odd parity, binary conversion, bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT, and logical left/right shifts; these map to the listed portable contracts, with a new explicit bit-vector zero-count contract. Source comparisons use bounded nonnegative canonical bit strings; AND is restricted to equal-width operands because the implementation assumes equal lengths and its shorter-width loop is inconsistent with its padding code. BitArray equality, ordering, enumeration, cloning, reset/set-all, and hash code are object/support operations without a standalone shared algorithm contract. The shift methods operate on MSB-first bit strings, appending or dropping low-order bits.

The pinned Java class exposes distinct `rotateLeft(int,int)` and `rotateRight(int,int)` 32-bit circular rotations. The benchmarks use the same 32-bit word, normalize a nonnegative shift modulo 32, and represent Java’s signed-int result as the corresponding unsigned 32-bit value in i64. The package bounds shift to nonnegative int32; list rotation and bit reversal are different operations.

The pinned Java method swaps the two selected 0-based bit positions in a signed 32-bit int and leaves data unchanged when those bits match; valid positions are 0..31. The benchmark returns the resulting int32 sign-extended to i64. Its invalid sentinel is -2147483649, outside all valid int32 results, because -1 is itself a valid output. This is distinct from swapping all adjacent bit pairs or swapping two integer values.

The pinned C# exact matcher returns the first lowercase-ASCII byte match and supports patterns through length 31. It shares the core operation with bitap_string_match but remains a separate contract because that package permits 63-character patterns.

The pinned Python source and nine ports implement exact first-match search over lowercase ASCII. Empty pattern returns 0; no match or a pattern longer than the text returns -1. The workload bounds the pattern to 63 characters for a portable 64-bit Bitap state. The separate C# `bitap` candidate has a 31-character limit and is not mapped to this wider contract.

The pinned Go source repeatedly shifts an unsigned value right and counts low set bits until zero. It returns the same population count as the canonical hamming_weight benchmark for portable unsigned 32-bit inputs; zero returns zero.

The pinned Python `AssignmentUsingBitmask` source counts injective person-to-task assignments by processing task IDs and memoizing `(assigned_people_mask, task_no)`. Each eligibility entry appends a person to a task's list, so duplicate IDs intentionally multiply counts; the benchmark preserves that behavior. Its bounded input uses up to 8 people, 12 tasks, and 12 entries per person, with task IDs in `1..total_tasks`; repeated entries are valid even when their count exceeds the number of tasks. The nine ports use the equivalent bounded task/mask recurrence.

The pinned Nim source repeatedly propagates carry with AND, combines non-carry bits with XOR, and shifts the carry left. The portable benchmark limits inputs to nonnegative signed-64 values whose sum fits, avoiding source-negative examples that would require signed-shift behavior.

The pinned Python function rejects negative inputs and recursively combines XOR with the shifted AND carry until carry is zero. The benchmark restricts both integer inputs to nonnegative signed-32-bit values and preserves that recurrence; the maximum result fits signed 64-bit.

The pinned Java source uses Stein’s binary GCD: remove common powers of two, reduce odd operands by subtraction, and restore the common shift. The shared domain is nonnegative signed-64-bit inputs, including gcd(0,0)=0, so the negative and Long.MIN_VALUE fallback paths are outside the contract. This is distinct from Euclid’s modulo-based `gcd` benchmark.

The pinned Go `Bitwise(a,b,base)` extracts bit 31 of a-b and returns a-(i*(a-b)). The benchmark fixes base=31 and restricts a,b to nonnegative int32 so the sign bit exactly selects the larger input without subtraction overflow. It models the source’s 32-bit variant; other tested base widths are excluded.

The pinned Go function folds a variadic list with a sign-bit mask, selecting between the running minimum and each next value without branches. On the benchmark’s bounded nonnegative signed-i32 domain, fixed shift base 31 matches the signed-int convention; the ports preserve the bitwise selection recurrence.

The pinned R source's European call and put methods use the Black-Scholes d1/d2 sequence and normal CDF formulas represented by this package. The benchmark normalizes the source class into an explicit option selector and rate, constrains inputs to a bounded three-decimal grid, and uses erfc for the equivalent normal CDF evaluation. The source's Greeks and implied-volatility methods are outside this contract.

The pinned Rust source implements the BLAKE2b compression with a configurable digest length and a key of up to 64 bytes. The shared benchmark selects the unkeyed 64-byte BLAKE2b-512 configuration and bounds input messages to 4,096 bytes. Nine portable language implementations use the same byte-array contract, 128-byte blocks, twelve rounds, and little-endian digest encoding.

The pinned MATLAB-Octave demos are toolbox-dependent frame examples. The canonical blobDetection.m uses HSV thresholds H=[0.379,0.496], S>=0.436; BlobUsingVideo.m uses H=[0.398,0.498], S>=0.355. Both open with a radius-3 disk and count 8-connected regions with inclusive area bounds 200 through 5000; BlobAnalysis defaults to at most 50 objects. The portable profile field preserves both threshold sets with exact rational comparisons and an exact Euclidean radius-3 disk (MATLAB strel defaults to a four-line approximation). Both demos are represented by this shared count contract. All nine ports passed 164 oracle arrays and 29 workload records.

This video-reader demo uses the same HSV segmentation, disk opening, 8-connected area filtering, and object count as blobDetection.m, but with a different tuned threshold set. It is represented by profile 1 in the shared blob_detection workload; video decoding and display are excluded.

The pinned implementations provide insertion and membership queries without deletion, though their hash functions and filter sizes differ. The shared contract starts a fresh 64-bit filter per call, uses operation/key pairs (1 inserts, 2 queries membership), keys 0..1,000,000,000, and a deterministic pair of hash positions. Each query emits one byte; invalid input returns -1 and insufficient output capacity returns -2.

This class does not implement standard Blowfish key expansion: keyGenerate only XORs the 18 P-array entries and never updates the four S-boxes with the evolving cipher output. Standard Blowfish expansion replaces all 18 P entries and 1024 S-box entries through 521 encryption operations. It also mutates subKeys across calls, so reusing an instance accumulates key state. Excluded as an invalid Blowfish implementation; no source-specific benchmark contract is defined.

This implementation does not perform the standard Blowfish key schedule: GenerateKey only XORs values into the P-array and never uses repeated encryption to replace the P-array and four S-boxes. Its key slicing also assumes each cyclic substring has eight characters, which fails for many valid key lengths and does not correctly cycle arbitrary-length key material. Excluded as an invalid Blowfish implementation; no source-specific benchmark contract is defined.

The pinned Java implementation indexes lowercase words from movie names and content, then returns documents containing one query term in descending BM25 score order using k1=1.5, b=0.75, and log(1 + (N-df+0.5)/(df+0.5)). The portable benchmark supplies normalized token IDs and ranks a single query; because its IDF is common and positive for every matching document, ports compare the exact rational term-frequency/document-length factor and break exact ties by ascending document ID. This avoids locale-dependent tokenization and floating-point ranking differences.

The pinned Swift Minimax Board checks whether the selected player has a full row, column, or either full-length diagonal; if not, it reports continues when any cell is empty and draw otherwise. The benchmark supplies a bounded row-major board directly and omits mutation/position helpers. Sizes start at 2 because the source row/column loops classify a size-one board as a win even when its sole cell is not the selected player.

The pinned Java methods `bpR`, `bpRS`, and `bpIS` all count ways to advance from start to end using die steps 1 through 6. The bounded contract preserves the equal-position result of one, the path-count recurrence, and the source's signed-int-safe maximum.
The pinned Swift source is a tuple type alias for a row and column in a Minimax playground model; it defines no standalone algorithm.
The pinned Swift source is a three-case status enum used by the Minimax playground model; it defines no standalone algorithm.
The pinned Swift source builds a UIKit game interface, handles button events, and updates views; it delegates Minimax moves to `GameModel` rather than implementing the search itself.
At the pinned Go revision, bom.go declares the package but every implementation and CLI/demo block is commented out; there is no active matching routine to port or benchmark.
The pinned C header defines a platform compatibility BOOL enum/typedef plus TRUE/FALSE conversion macros for a client/server example; it contains no standalone algorithm.

The pinned Java class implements AND, OR, NOT, XOR, NAND, and NOR over Boolean inputs. The benchmark assigns explicit gate codes, preserves empty-list identities for the five list gates, and requires exactly one input for NOT; all values and malformed cases use a bounded integer-array adapter.
The pinned Python source implements Booth’s linear-time lexicographically minimal string rotation algorithm. This is distinct from Booth’s multiplication algorithm.

The pinned Python Graph.boruvka selects a cheapest outgoing edge per component, unions selected component pairs, and reports total MST weight. It aliases boruvkas_minimum_spanning_tree for connected simple positive-weight graphs; the shared contract excludes the Python source's non-progressing disconnected case and reduces insertion-order tie differences to total weight.

The pinned Java boruvkaMST selects the cheapest outgoing edge for each union-find component and returns an MST edge list. It aliases boruvkas_minimum_spanning_tree on the shared connected simple positive-weight graph domain; the benchmark compares total weight rather than source-specific edge-list order.

The pinned C++ sources use Borůvka phases: each component selects its cheapest outgoing edge, then components are merged. The bounded simple connected graph contract preserves distinct edges and deterministic weight ordering.

The pinned Java method fills every 8-connected non-boundary pixel reachable from a seed, mutating the image in place. The port contract encodes Java's image[x][y] in x-major order and adds upper-bound checks because the source recurses beyond the array when the fill reaches its right or bottom edge. All nine portable ports passed the 10 workload cases.

The pinned Java recursive method emits a nonleaf root, the left boundary preferring left children, all leaves left-to-right, and the right boundary in reverse while preferring right children. When the root has no left child, the source includes the right path as the left boundary and skips the right-boundary pass to avoid duplicates. The portable indexed-tree contract validates one reachable rooted tree, bounds values to signed 32-bit, and requires output capacity for at least the node count.

The C++, C# Strings/PatternMatching, Java searches, and JavaScript sources perform full Boyer–Moore string matching with both bad-character and good-suffix shifts. This is distinct from boyer_moore_search, which applies only the bad-character rule, and from the majority-vote algorithm. The shared contract returns the first match over ASCII bytes 0..126 and treats an empty pattern as a match at index zero.

The pinned Python file includes first-match and all-match variants. The all-match routine builds Horspool shifts from pattern bytes except the final byte, compares each window right-to-left, and shifts using the text byte aligned with the pattern's final byte. It advances one byte after a match to retain overlaps, and an empty pattern matches every text boundary. The benchmark follows this all-match behavior over ASCII bytes with explicit-length inputs.

The pinned Ruby source is a variant of Boyer–Moore–Horspool, but its shift table includes the final pattern byte, allowing a zero shift, and it looks up the mismatching byte rather than the byte at the window end. The benchmark maps this filename to the intended Horspool algorithm implemented by the Python source; the README records the source divergence.

The pinned C-Sharp and Java BoyerMoore sources use Boyer-Moore majority cancellation and verify that the candidate occurs more than half the time. The shared contract allows no-majority inputs and returns -1 for them. The same C-Sharp and Java repositories also contain separate full string-search implementations, which map to the boyer_moore benchmark.

Inspected the pinned C, Python, and Rust sources. Each uses the Boyer-Moore bad-character rule; C prints matches while Python and Rust return match-position lists, and Rust uses Unicode character positions. The shared benchmark accepts ASCII byte sequences packed as text length, pattern length, and payload; it returns the first match index, defines an empty pattern as a match at zero, and returns -1 for malformed input or no match. Nine portable implementations use a 128-entry last-occurrence table.

The pinned Go `BoyerMoore` source uses an Apostolico–Giancarlo suffix-memory table over bad-character shifts. It returns all matches, advances one position after a match to preserve overlaps, and rejects the empty pattern because the source loop would not advance. This is distinct from pure Horspool and the standard full Boyer–Moore package.

The pinned Python source validates exactly three positive pressure/volume values, solves the missing variable from p1*v1=p2*v2, formats the binary64 quotient to three decimal places, and parses it back. The shared benchmark instead defines exact-rational ties-to-even rounding so all nine ports agree; README/workload document the known discriminator [3,1,80,1] (benchmark 0.012, Python .3f 0.013).

The pinned Python Tokenizer starts from UTF-8 bytes, counts adjacent token pairs in encounter order, selects the most frequent pair with first-seen tie-breaking, and merges non-overlapping occurrences left to right using token ID 256 plus the merge step. The portable benchmark accepts the already encoded byte sequence, bounds it to 512 bytes and 32 merges, and returns little-endian u16 token IDs; text encoding and decoding are outside the measured operation. All nine ports passed 7,020 oracle cases and 19 workload cases.

The pinned Python source computes sine=(order*wavelength)/(2*distance), rejects values outside [-1,1], applies asin and degrees, then rounds to one decimal place. The benchmark records a bounded integer-picometre subset and explicitly defines a shared scale-first ties-to-even rounding rule; this can differ from Python near binary64 decimal midpoints and is documented as a normalized cross-language contract.

The pinned Python BraikMac builds the five source column-replacement matrices and returns their signed determinants as six formatted conic coefficients. The portable benchmark restricts the five points to integer coordinates in -10..10 and returns the exact six signed determinants before display formatting, avoiding floating-point and formatting differences while preserving the source matrix layouts and signs. All nine ports passed 1,300 oracle cases and 13 workload cases.

The pinned Lua source interprets Brainfuck byte commands with bracket pairing, byte cells, input/output, and a tape pointer. The portable benchmark accepts printable ASCII programs and arbitrary input bytes, ignores non-command characters, uses byte wrapping, and makes the source tape finite with positions -128..128 plus explicit 100,000-step and 8,192-output-byte limits. Malformed programs and bound violations return -2. All nine ports passed the independent bytecode oracle and published workloads.

The pinned C# generic solver explores include/exclude nodes breadth-first, computes a fractional-knapsack bound, and returns its chosen items by walking the best path backward. Its `OrderBy(value / weight)` sorts density ascending, so the purported upper bound can underestimate the optimum; the input [(1,1),(1,1),(1,2)] at capacity 1 returns value 1 instead of 2. The portable benchmark corrects the ordering to stable descending density, limits inputs to eight items with positive integer weights and values, and emits selected input IDs in reverse density-path order. The separate BranchAndBoundNode source is a helper record, not another solver.
The pinned C# source stores knapsack search-tree state such as level, weight, value, bound, and parent; it contains no branch-and-bound search procedure.

The pinned C++ implementation supports directed or bidirectional edges and returns all visited vertices; the Rust implementation uses directed edges and returns history only until a requested target. The shared contract normalizes both APIs to a complete directed traversal in deterministic ascending-neighbor order.

The pinned Python file implements full reachable-vertex BFS twice, using Queue and deque. Both mark vertices explored when enqueued, append each first discovery to the result, and preserve outgoing adjacency-list order. The shared contract normalizes neighbor order to ascending vertex IDs, matching its deterministic cross-language traversal convention.

The pinned Python source traverses a directed string-label graph in adjacency-list order, recording first-discovery parents. The shared contract normalizes labels to bounded integer IDs and returns the first shortest path as a vertex vector; source==target returns [source], unreachable returns [0].

The pinned Python file contains two operations. Its path-returning bfs_shortest_path function matches the separate path-vector contract after string/list output normalization; its bfs_shortest_path_distance helper returns edge count and is tracked as a separate scalar benchmark with single-character labels because the source initializes visited from set(start).

The pinned Python source uses deque-based 0–1 BFS, pushing zero-cost improvements to the front and one-cost improvements to the back, and returns the shortest distance. The package preserves this result on bounded directed graphs with weights 0 or 1, maps unreachable targets to -1, and rejects malformed endpoints or weights through the ABI.

The pinned JavaScript function queues candidate paths in FIFO order, expands outgoing neighbors in array order, immediately returns [start] for equal endpoints, returns the first shortest target path, and returns [] when unreachable. Those behaviors match the existing directed ordered-neighbor shortest-path contract, which projects paths to integer vertex IDs and encodes unreachable as [0].

The pinned C# and JavaScript sources perform ordinary binary-tree level order, enqueuing left then right and returning node payloads. Both map to mode 3 of the shared binary_tree_traversal contract on valid trees.

The pinned Go source uses an adjacency matrix and returns `(connected, distance)`, counting unweighted edge hops. Its API maps to the directed shortest-path distance contract for valid square nonnegative matrices and in-range endpoints. The benchmark returns the distance when connected, zero for equal endpoints, and -1 when distinct endpoints are unreachable; the source reports `(false, 0)` for both equal endpoints and unreachable cases, so that projection is applied only on the shared contract domain.
The pinned Python source combines inverse quadratic interpolation, secant steps, and guarded bisection fallback, preserving its default tolerance, iteration cap, and final-right-endpoint return.

The pinned C++ sources use Brent's parabolic interpolation with golden-section fallback to find extrema. The bounded float64 contract selects among (x-2)^2, cos(x), and -cos(x), validates the bracket, and caps iteration at 256. The source's mislabeled cosine test is documented; this extrema search is distinct from the Python brent_method root finder.

The pinned Java source uses integer error accumulation with strict `e2 > -dy` and `e2 < dx` conditions and emits both endpoints inclusively; a zero-length segment emits one point. This is distinct from the floating-increment DDA rasterizer, which has different endpoint and degenerate behavior.

The pinned Python classic rasterizer uses the `p = 2*dy - dx` update and advances y when `p >= 0`. On its documented domain (x1 <= x2 and 0 <= dy <= dx), it matches the inclusive-tie `bresenhams_line` contract; the shared contract generalizes to all slopes and directions. The source file also contains an optional Matplotlib demo.

The pinned Python generalized rasterizer uses absolute deltas, signed steps, and strict doubled-error comparisons (`e2 > -dy` and `e2 < dx`), matching the `bresenham_line` tie pixels in every direction. The shared contract adds portable coordinate bounds and a fixed binary output format. The source file also contains an optional Matplotlib demo.

The pinned Nim source uses Bresenham error updates with inclusive comparisons (`doubleDifference >= dy` and `doubleDifference <= dx`). Those tie choices can emit different raster pixels from the strict-comparison Java bresenham_line candidate, so this is a separate benchmark with the Nim tie contract.

The pinned Java countSetBits repeatedly clears the lowest set bit with `num &= num - 1`, matching method selector 0 in the canonical set-bit-count benchmark for nonnegative signed-i32 inputs. Negative Java ints use their 32-bit two's-complement representation, which is outside the shared nonnegative domain.

The pinned Kotlin BrickSort implementation is named oddEvenSort and alternates odd-indexed and even-indexed adjacent compare-and-swap passes until a pass pair makes no swaps. It is the same odd-even transposition sort as odd_even_sort.

The pinned R `BridgeDetector` uses Tarjan discovery and low-link values and searches all graph components. Its native endpoint orientation and result order may vary, so the shared contract normalizes each undirected edge and sorts the output.

The two pinned C++ files are mirrored Tarjan cut-edge implementations, but explicitly assume a connected graph and begin DFS at vertex 0. The benchmark searches every component and normalizes output edge orientation and order; this source-name candidate aliases the canonical bridges contract.

The pinned C# source applies Tarjan discovery-time and low-link rules to report cut edges across connected components. The shared contract normalizes each undirected edge to `(min,max)`, sorts results lexicographically, coalesces duplicate inputs, and visits every component for deterministic output.

The pinned MATLAB-Octave source classifies an RGB triple by the nearest of 11 fixed labeled RGB samples. The benchmark preserves sample order and first-row tie resolution; squared integer Euclidean distances preserve the nearest-sample ordering without floating-point or hardware-specific operations. Inputs are bounded to byte-valued RGB channels.

The pinned Java source copies neighbor sets, removes self-edges, then uses pivoted Bron–Kerbosch recursion to enumerate every maximal clique. The shared contract bounds symmetric undirected graphs to five vertices and encodes the complete maximal-clique set as a bitset indexed by vertex masks; this avoids source HashSet iteration-order differences while preserving the exact output set.

The pinned Python helper tries Caesar decryption keys 0 through 25, shifting uppercase ASCII letters backward and preserving other bytes. The package emits the 26 candidate plaintext rows in key order, without the source display labels.

The pinned Java source uses direct recursive include/exclude search for 0/1 knapsack without memoization. Each item is used at most once; the bounded item count keeps the exponential workload tractable and the result in the source int range.

The pinned C++ brute_force(text, pattern) compares every candidate substring and returns the first matching index or -1; an empty pattern returns 0. This matches the shared direct-scan benchmark on its bounded NUL-free ASCII input domain.

The pinned Ruby class implements a unique-key unbalanced BST with insert, delete, membership, minimum, maximum, size, and traversal operations. It maps to the existing ordered-set operation trace when insert keys are distinct and deletes target present keys. Duplicate insertion increments its size then raises, so duplicate-insert behavior is outside this Ruby source mapping; tree shape and successor choice do not affect the shared observable results.

The pinned Java implementation recursively chooses start + (end - start) / 2 for each sorted slice, producing the lower midpoint for even lengths. The shared contract accepts strictly increasing signed 32-bit inputs and encodes the resulting implicit heap-index tree shape; empty and null source inputs both denote an empty tree.

The pinned Java class iteratively implements add, remove, and find for integer keys. Duplicate insertion is ignored and removing an absent key leaves the set unchanged, matching the existing ordered-set state semantics. Its mapping is limited to traces using insert, delete, and search operations; the benchmark's minimum, maximum, and size operations are not in this source API. Console messages and void add/remove return types are adapter details outside the shared contract.
The pinned PHP file defines binary-search-tree node storage and predicates only; it contains no tree insertion, search, traversal, or other benchmarkable algorithm.

The pinned Java class recursively implements add, remove, and find for integer keys. Insertions of existing keys and removals of absent keys leave the tree unchanged, matching the existing ordered-set state semantics. Its mapping is limited to traces using insert, delete, and search operations; the benchmark's minimum, maximum, and size operations are not in this source API. Console messages and void add/remove return types are adapter details outside the shared contract.

The pinned Java class implements a recursive generic BST ordered by Comparable, with add, remove, find, and sorted traversal. For integer keys, duplicate insertion and absent-key removal are no-ops, matching the existing ordered-set state semantics. Its mapping is limited to traces using insert, delete, and search operations; the benchmark's minimum, maximum, and size operations are not in this source API. Generic type behavior and console messages are outside the shared signed-integer contract.

The pinned Go source implements an ordered generic key set with unique insertion, lookup, deletion, extrema, and traversals. The PHP BSTree stores values under integer keys, supports search/removal, and throws on duplicate insertion. Both map to the existing integer ordered-set contract on traces with unique insertions and known-present deletes; PHP values are outside the key-only contract. Tree shape and successor choice are not compared.

The pinned C#, Go, Java, and Lua sources all support ordered B-tree set operations. The contract uses unique signed-i32 keys, fresh inserts, membership queries, and deletes only for keys known present, then returns query results and ordered remaining keys. Duplicate inserts and missing deletes are excluded because source behavior differs. Lua's default order holds 509 keys in one node, so workloads exceed that size to exercise splitting; C# uses minimum degree 2, Go is configured with a valid max-key count, and Java uses a supported degree.
The pinned C# source represents a B-tree node and provides local key/child setters and shifts, but no tree search, split, insertion, or deletion algorithm at this file boundary.

The checked C and C++ implementations compare adjacent values, swap out-of-order pairs, and stop early after a pass without swaps. The local contract sorts signed 64-bit values in ascending order in place and is stable.
The pinned PHP implementation repeatedly compares adjacent values and swaps inversions until a pass makes no swaps, matching bubble_sort.

The pinned C implementation repeatedly scans its fixed 20-element demo array, swapping adjacent inversions until no swap occurs. It is standard bubble sort; its fixed demo-size API does not alter the shared variable-length contract.
The pinned C implementation performs one adjacent-swap pass and recurses on the shortened prefix only when that pass swaps values, matching the early-exit recursive bubble_sort_recursive benchmark.

The pinned Java and Python sources perform one adjacent-swap pass and recurse on the shortened prefix only if a swap occurred. The Java version mutates in place; Python slices the prefix and returns a new list. The shared contract uses in-place sorting of signed 64-bit values and caps length at 256. The early-exit behavior distinguishes it from recursive_bubble_sort, which recurses after every pass.
The pinned C-Sharp class implements adjacent-swap bubble sort with an early exit after a pass makes no swaps. It shares the canonical bubble_sort ordering contract and workload.

Go Bubble and Lua bubblesort repeatedly compare adjacent values and exchange inversions, so they use the same stable bubble-sort contract. The Go implementation exits early after a pass without swaps; the Lua version runs fixed passes.

Despite its class name, the pinned C-Sharp implementation distributes values into ten buckets on each successive decimal digit and collects them between passes. That is least-significant-digit radix sort, not range bucket_sort; it is grouped with radix_sort, whose shared contract extends the supported domain to signed 64-bit values.

The pinned Go implementation maps the numeric range into n buckets, insertion-sorts each bucket, then concatenates them, matching bucket_sort. Its range formula divides by max-min without handling a uniform input, so equal-only inputs can trigger invalid division; the shared contract handles that case.

The pinned Java file implements a byte-stream BufferedReader utility with read, peek, availability, and block operations. Its behavior is tied to the supplied InputStream contract rather than a standalone algorithm, so it is excluded from the algorithm benchmark set.
The pinned Zig source is the repository build script that selects algorithm modules and registers test steps; it is build tooling rather than an algorithm.

The pinned Python source runs five rounds with random bases in rabin_miller and screens with small primes through 997 in is_prime_low_num. It is mapped to the shared Miller–Rabin benchmark, which normalizes randomized/configurable witnesses to fixed bases [2, 3, 5, 7] over the signed 32-bit domain. The raw rabin_miller primitive is not called on inputs below 3 because its small-input behavior is undefined; the benchmark's valid-domain guard handles values below 2.

The pinned Python function rejects nonpositive concentrations, then requires donor and acceptor concentrations to exceed intrinsic concentration. It returns Boltzmann * 300 * log((donor * acceptor) / intrinsic**2) divided by the SciPy electron-volt constant; the package uses the bounded positive integer subset and preserves this operation order.

The pinned Python class converts BGR pixels to grayscale, scans row-major, thresholds to black or white, and distributes quantization error to two following pixels on the current row and five pixels on the next row using Burkes weights. The shared contract uses exact rational grayscale coefficients and integer truncation toward zero to keep all ports deterministic, while preserving scan, threshold, and error-spread order; it uses square inputs to avoid the source's reversed output dimensions.

The pinned R function appends `$`, sorts all cyclic rotations, and returns the augmented original, rotations, and last column. Its core last-column transform maps to the case-sensitive BWT contract when adapting input as text + `$` and normalizing sorting to the benchmark's ordinal byte order. R's default locale-sensitive sort is not equivalent on every environment, so parity requires that explicit ordering normalization. The source returns additional representations that are outside the BWT output contract.

The pinned Python source implements the same case-sensitive cyclic-rotation Burrows–Wheeler transform as the canonical C#, Java, and Rust compression sources. Its return shape is normalized to the shared last-column plus original-row result.

The C#, Java, and Rust compression sources implement case-sensitive cyclic-rotation BWT and return the last column plus original row index. Rust's separate string module sorts rotation keys case-insensitively and can differ on mixed-case inputs such as `aA`, so it maps to its own additional benchmark.

The pinned Go MaxCoins source pads the values with boundary ones and fills an interval table in increasing span. Each candidate balloon is considered as the last burst in its interval, so the left and right subinterval scores are independent and the boundary product is added. The empty input returns zero; the benchmark preserves that behavior and bounds values to 0..1000 and length to 128 so signed 64-bit products and totals are safe.

The pinned Python source returns an ASCII string with star wings for rows 1 through n-1, a solid row of 2n-1 stars, and the mirrored lower rows. The portable contract preserves this row and spacing order, uses newline separators without a trailing newline, and bounds n to 1..45 so the maximum output fits the shared 8,192-byte ABI buffer.

The pinned Python module defines nine second-order filter factories and stores coefficients in IIRFilter without normalizing by a0. The benchmark selects one coefficient from the ordered a0..a2,b0..b2 arrays, preserves the RBJ formulas, source Q default, and gain handling, and imposes a shared bounded frequency domain. make_notch and make_bandpass_peak omit the source's common validation call, so their adapter inputs are restricted to the same valid design domain.

The pinned C++ implementations return whether n is divisible by 7 or has a final decimal digit of 7. Under signed remainders, a negative value ending in 7 does not satisfy the second condition; the shared signed 64-bit contract preserves that behavior.

The pinned C# utility reads unsigned 64-bit values from big-endian byte spans and writes them to big-endian spans. The scalar benchmark represents the input span as a little-endian-packed signed i64 and transports the UInt64 bits through the ABI as signed i64; reversing all eight bytes therefore models both BigEndianToUint64 and UInt64ToBigEndian without signed arithmetic.

The pinned C source parses an ASCII C string using six-byte whitespace skipping, one optional sign, and the longest initial decimal run, stopping at NUL. The shared contract defines signed-32 saturation and malformed-byte handling; its NUL and whitespace rules make it distinct from string_to_integer.

The pinned Go, Java, Julia, Ruby, and Rust files are variants of the Caesar substitution cipher. They differ in shift limits, letter case, and nonletter handling, so this filename candidate shares the standardized ASCII contract and workload with caesar_cipher.

The pinned C++, JavaScript, PHP, and Python files implement Caesar substitution but differ in case handling, configurable alphabets, and shift validation. The shared benchmark specifies ASCII upper/lowercase rotation, leaves other ASCII bytes unchanged, and normalizes every signed 64-bit shift modulo 26.

The pinned C# CaesarEncoder shifts ASCII letters while preserving case and leaves other ASCII unchanged. Its signed key bound of ±1,000,000 keeps source integer arithmetic in range and matches the shared caesar_cipher contract after modulo-26 normalization.
The pinned C-Sharp sequence emits the cake-number formula at zero-based indices beginning with 1. The bounded scalar contract and all nine ports use the same exact integer formula.
The pinned TypeScript calculate_mean source computes the arithmetic mean and maps to the canonical binary64 average contract.

The pinned TypeScript source indexes the middle element of an already sorted array, or averages the central pair for even lengths. The benchmark preserves direct indexing as an O(1) operation by making sortedness and signed-i32 range preconditions; it returns twice the statistical median so half-integer results remain exact in the integer ABI.

The pinned Python source converts camel/Pascal case to snake_case by inserting underscores before uppercase ASCII letters and lowercasing them. The letter-only input domain avoids the source's mixed-character indexing edge cases and is distinct from the inverse conversion.

The pinned Python source lowercases its text and removes spaces before checking whether at most one character count is odd. The benchmark contract is limited to nonempty lowercase ASCII letters, where those preprocessing steps do not alter the input and the predicate matches the portable frequency-count implementations.

The pinned Python source blurs a grayscale image with a 9×9 Gaussian kernel and edge replication, computes absolute Sobel components, independently normalizes them, forms and normalizes the gradient magnitude, applies directional non-maximum suppression, thresholds at 15/30, then performs one row-major hysteresis pass. The benchmark uses deterministic fixed-point arithmetic and a side-bounded byte-image contract; it safely limits the upstream out-of-bounds hysteresis scan to interior pixels and preserves the one-pass order. The OpenCV demo imports are excluded.

The pinned C program prints each retained interval after every Cantor-set propagation level, with `%lf` endpoints at six decimal places and a blank line between levels. The package preserves that byte format on its bounded integer endpoints and levels.

The pinned Python module computes parallel capacitance with a sequential sum and series capacitance as the reciprocal of a sequential sum of reciprocals. Parallel mode allows zero but rejects negative values; series mode rejects zero and negatives. The benchmark selects the source function by operation and uses bounded nonempty integer-valued inputs.

The pinned F# and Python helpers capitalize only the initial character. On the shared bounded ASCII-byte domain, an initial lowercase ASCII letter is uppercased and all remaining bytes are preserved. This differs from the word-by-word title_case_conversion benchmark.

The pinned Dart source uses a fixed passenger difference timeline and returns whether capacity is respected. Its cumulative scan starts at stop 1, which skips occupancy on [0,1); the shared contract preserves the timeline method and corrects this source defect by checking every occupied segment from stop 0.

The pinned Python source tests the universal Fermat congruence for every coprime base from 2 through n-1 using modular exponentiation by squaring. Its `all()` predicate also accepts primes and the empty-base cases n=1 and n=2; the benchmark adds n>=3 and a compositeness check to identify Carmichael numbers specifically, bounded to 10,000.

The pinned C source and header define a fixed-capacity integer-array API with insert, remove, update, push, erase, reverse, three sorting methods, searches, copying, display, and a time-seeded random shuffle. This filename is a collection of data-structure operations rather than one standalone algorithm with a single bounded input/output contract; its sorting and search methods are separate algorithm candidates.

The pinned Python function requires exactly one zero and nonnegative concentrations. It returns a `(field_name, value)` tuple; the bounded package uses the zero's input position to encode the missing field and returns the corresponding scalar, so the field label is recoverable from the input. It preserves the three source formulas and branch order.
