The pinned TypeScript function rejects negative or nonintegral inputs and repeatedly adds the last decimal digit before flooring division by ten. It matches sum_of_digits on the shared bounded nonnegative integer domain.

The pinned Python DDA source computes the dominant-axis step count, repeatedly adds binary64 x/y increments, applies Python ties-to-even rounding after each addition, omits the start point, and includes the endpoint. The benchmark rejects zero-length lines to avoid division by zero and bounds steps to 4,096; it remains distinct from integer-error Bresenham line drawing.

The pinned Java and Python sources repeatedly sum decimal digits until one digit remains. The Ruby add_digits candidates implement the same mathematical operation, using either recursive repeated summation or the modulo-nine digital-root identity. The benchmark uses the repeated-sum variant, accepts nonnegative signed-64-bit inputs, and returns -1 for negative inputs.

The inspected C source uses an adjacency matrix, signed int distances, and a static remembered minimum-vertex index; C++ uses a priority queue for a source-to-target query but stores queue distances as int while its distance vector is int64_t; Rust returns a predecessor map for reachable vertices using an ordered set. The local contract standardizes all-source distances, nonnegative signed 64-bit weights, and explicit overflow and invalid-input statuses. Nine ports use the same flat-edge-list, no-allocation minimum-selection variant.

The pinned Python source uses a square adjacency matrix with floating-point storage and prints a distance for every vertex. It is equivalent on simple directed graphs with nonnegative integral weights and distances exactly representable in binary64 (at most 2^53); its `inf` sentinel represents unreachable vertices. Its -1 minimum fallback after reachable vertices are exhausted only scans an unreachable row and cannot improve a distance on this nonnegative domain.

The pinned C#, Java, and Python sources compute single-source shortest paths; the benchmark uses connected undirected simple graphs on at most four dense vertices, source 0, and positive bounded weights. The bound keeps Python’s custom decrease-key priority queue from reaching the incorrect-parent region, avoids its zero-initialized distances for unrepresented vertices, and satisfies C#’s initial queue assumption that the source has index 0.

The pinned Python source is adjacency-matrix Dijkstra with 0 denoting no edge and a 10,000,000 distance sentinel. It matches the shared directed-distance contract on simple graphs with positive integral edge weights and every reachable shortest distance below 10,000,000; the source prints distances while the shared ABI returns them.

The pinned Python source runs heap-based Dijkstra over walkable cells in a binary grid, with unit-cost orthogonal or diagonal moves, and returns one source-to-destination distance and path. It is the same shortest-path operation on an implicitly represented unit-weight graph; the shared flat-edge contract represents each walkable cell as a vertex and compares the destination distance, ignoring path tie order.

The pinned C++ graph wrapper allocates empty distance and visited vectors, then indexes them as if they had V elements in dijkstra(); the first initialization writes out of bounds, so the implementation has undefined behavior on every nonempty graph and cannot be benchmarked as a working source.

The pinned R source uses a vector-backed priority queue and returns distances plus predecessors. It matches the shared distance result for valid one-based contiguous vertex IDs, nonnegative integral weights, and distances exactly representable by R doubles; predecessor choices and the example/demo are outside the distance contract.

The pinned JavaScript source grows source-to-vertex paths by repeatedly choosing the cheapest outgoing edge from the discovered frontier. On simple directed graphs with nonnegative bounded weights and numeric vertex IDs it yields the same reachable shortest distances; the shared contract normalizes IDs and represents omitted unreachable vertices with reachability flags, while path tie order is ignored.

The pinned PHP source performs single-source relaxation over an edge list and repeatedly chooses the least-distance unvisited vertex. It matches the shared contract for nonempty graphs with unique declared vertex names (including the source), valid endpoints, nonnegative weights, and finite distances below the platform integer sentinel; names and returned array keys are normalized to vertex IDs.

The pinned Python source is Dijkstra's two-stack arithmetic-expression evaluator, not graph shortest paths. It scans a fully parenthesized infix expression, pushes single-digit operands and four arithmetic operators, and evaluates on closing parentheses; the benchmark preserves the algorithm on valid bounded expressions with exact integer division.

The pinned Python dilation routine multiplies each image neighborhood by the structuring element and emits 1 when the sum is positive. The bounded benchmark fixes a zero-padded 3x3 kernel and binary image/kernel values, preserving source placement and kernel order while avoiding the source invalid dimension-1 slicing behavior. The byte-output oracle, nine ports, and verifier corpus follow this contract.

The pinned Python module is an umbrella. Its PCA, LDA, and seeded t-SNE methods are split into separate bounded contracts at benchmarks/d/dimensionality_reduction_pca/README.md, benchmarks/d/dimensionality_reduction_lda/README.md, and benchmarks/d/dimensionality_reduction_tsne/README.md. The t-SNE split fixes the seed to 42, the input to one feature and three samples, perplexity 1.5, learning rate 10, and five iterations; it preserves the source's binary-search conditional probabilities, symmetrization, Student-t affinities, momentum, and gradient update. The three initial embedding draws are fixed to NumPy's default_rng(42) output for this exact shape. Covariance helpers are support routines, not independent benchmark contracts.

The pinned R source is only four top-level statements: it loads stats, calls princomp(train, cor = TRUE), and predicts scores for train and test. It defines no function or input contract and depends on ambient train/test variables, so it is a dataset-workflow snippet rather than a self-contained algorithm implementation. Its operation is correlation-based PCA, but it is not an alias of the R pca_algorithm candidate: that function accepts X and k and returns reduced scores, components, and eigenvalues. No mapped benchmark package exists locally.

This candidate tracks the pinned Python module’s one-component PCA path only: feature-by-sample orientation, centered covariance with divisor N, and projection of the original uncentered input. The benchmark canonicalizes the eigenvector sign and bounds the matrix to two features and 2–8 samples. LDA and t-SNE remain separate uncovered methods in the umbrella dimensionality_reduction candidate.

The pinned Java and Python sources implement Dinic maximum flow and share the bounded scalar contract with the Rust canonical package; source indexing and residual representation differences are documented.
The pinned R source implements Dinic maximum flow and shares the bounded scalar contract with the Rust canonical package; its 1-based matrix representation and cut metadata are documented.

The pinned Rust implementation uses Dinic level graphs and blocking-flow DFS. Java, both pinned Python implementations, and R implement the same maximum-flow scalar under the bounded contract, with source-specific vertex indexing and residual representations documented in the guide.

The pinned Python diophantine(a,b,c) calls extended_gcd(a,b), asserts divisibility, scales the Bézout coefficients by c/d, and returns one pair as floats. For the solver contract subset a,b >= 0, (a,b) != (0,0), and |a|,|b|<=1000, |c|<=10000, Python extended_gcd has the same recursive quotient/remainder recurrence and selected coefficients as the pinned Java LinearDiophantineEquationsSolver, and its float scaling is exact throughout these bounds. The existing solver benchmark therefore represents this single-solution API on that subset; the Dart linear_diophantine_eqn benchmark only returns solvability. The file also contains diophantine_all_soln, which prints a requested arithmetic progression of solutions, and all_diophantine_solutions, which returns up to n signed integer pairs and handles (0,0,0) specially. Those enumeration/output APIs are not represented by the single-solution alias; extending coverage to them would be a separate contract, not an equivalence claim.

The pinned Python file defines reusable DirectedGraph and Graph adjacency-list classes, not merely a demo. Both store (weight, neighbor) records, suppress exact duplicate weighted pairs, allow distinct parallel weights, and remove every edge between a selected endpoint pair. DirectedGraph adds one orientation; Graph adds/removes both orientations (a self-loop is stored once). It also bundles traversal, degree, topological, and cycle routines, which are outside this mapping. The existing graph_lua_directed_weighted operation trace represents the shared storage subset: nodes are pre-created, weights are bounded numeric values, each current ordered pair has at most one edge, add_pair is used only for absent pairs (mapped to set_weight), remove_pair maps to remove_edge, and get_weight/has_edge/final enumeration map to the corresponding trace queries. For Graph, undirected pairs are encoded as symmetric directed edges and the two orientations are updated atomically with no intervening query; self-loops use one orientation. The subset excludes multiple distinct weights on the same endpoint pair, insertion-ordered all_nodes behavior, traversal/graph algorithms, and random graph generation/timing helpers.

This is a reusable generic directed graph ADT backed by Map keys and Set-valued adjacency, not a demo record. The existing graph_lua_directed_weighted operation trace covers its portable edge-store subset: insertEdge maps to storing boolean true, adjacentNodes membership is observable through edge queries, and edges maps to final edge enumeration. Set union coalesces repeated Haskell edges, matching idempotent boolean set_weight. The contract does not represent Haskell-only deleteNode or transpose behavior, or the nodes operation's isolated-node enumeration.

This is a reusable fixed-capacity directed weighted graph backed by an adjacency matrix, not an interface/demo record. The existing graph_lua_directed_weighted contract covers the edge-operation subset when all vertices are created before the trace, edge additions use unique nonzero integer weights, and vertex additions/removals are omitted: AddEdge maps to numeric set_weight, RemoveEdge to remove_edge, AreAdjacent to has_edge, AdjacentDistance to get_weight, and GetNeighbors to the source-sorted outgoing edges. The contract does not model C# vertex capacity, ownership checks, or RemoveVertex index compaction.

The pinned Python function sums decimal digits raised to their one-based positions and matches the existing disarium_number benchmark over 1..99,999,999. Python returns true for zero, while the Java-backed benchmark rejects nonpositive values; the alias is limited to the shared positive bounded domain.

The pinned Java predicate raises for nonpositive inputs and sums each decimal digit raised to its one-based position from the left. The shared contract preserves that predicate and bounds inputs to positive values whose digit-power sum fits signed 32-bit arithmetic.

The pinned Python and Java implementations sum each decimal digit raised to its 1-based position from the left and compare the sum with the input. They match the existing disarium_number predicate on the shared positive domain 1..99,999,999. Python returns false for inputs below 1; Java throws for nonpositive input, which is normalized by the shared contract.

Reviewed all seven pinned disjoint_set sources in C++ (two repositories), C-Sharp, Julia, PHP, Python, and TypeScript. They implement the same partition and set-union behavior as union_find, with path compression plus rank or size heuristics in most versions; C++ uses a one-based universe, while object-based versions carry values in nodes. This candidate aliases the shared zero-based union_find contract.
The pinned PHP source stores rank, payload, and a self-parent reference; union and find operations are implemented elsewhere.

Reviewed the pinned Java and Rust disjoint_set_union sources. Both implement the same partition and merge behavior as union_find, using node objects and rank in Java and indexed nodes with union by size in Rust. This candidate aliases the shared zero-based union_find contract.

The pinned Java class is a generic-node disjoint-set union using path compression and union by size. It maps to the shared bounded partition trace after mapping each input index to a singleton node; representative object identity and tree shape are ignored.

The pinned Ruby class creates singleton nodes, finds representatives with path compression, and unions by rank. The benchmark's integer IDs map to node identities; representatives and rank fields are not compared.

The pinned Haskell functions compute population variance as the mean squared deviation from the arithmetic mean and standard deviation as its square root. The contract returns variance followed by standard deviation; the bounded nonempty integer sample domain avoids the source division-by-zero case.

The candidate combines two unrelated filename matches. The pinned Go geometry source is Euclidean distance and aliases `euclidean_distance`; the pinned PHP string source is byte-string Levenshtein distance and maps to the additional `levenshtein_distance` benchmark.

The pinned Java source computes deltaX=x2-x1 and deltaY=y2-y1, then returns sqrt(deltaX*deltaX+deltaY*deltaY). The benchmark uses bounded integer coordinates, preserving exact differences and squared sums before binary64 square root, and returns a finite sentinel for malformed or out-of-range input.

The pinned Java class contains Euclidean, Manhattan, Hamming, and Minkowski methods. The Euclidean benchmark preserves the source typo dY = y2 - x1. Manhattan and Minkowski map to their established benchmarks on bounded source-compatible inputs. Java hammingDistance sums absolute differences in equal-length int arrays; its binary-vector subset maps to the fixed 64-bit Hamming benchmark. All nine target-language distance_formula ABI implementations compile and link.
The pinned C# source is a Dijkstra result record holding a vertex, predecessor, and distance; it contains no shortest-path procedure.

The pinned Python implementation uses the same postorder subtree-excess and absolute edge-flow algorithm as C LeetCode 979. Its recursive helper contributes each child's absolute excess and returns subtree coin count minus node count; it is cataloged as an alias of candidate 979.

The pinned Solidity contract exposes two state setters and a separate division getter; the observed result depends on prior contract state and transaction sequence, so it has no single-call deterministic algorithm contract.

The pinned Julia function enumerates all positive divisors of n in ascending order and rejects n <= 0. The benchmark maps that complete set losslessly to a positive signed-64-bit bit mask for 1 <= n <= 62; the bit-mask representation is documented by the contract.

The pinned C# lazy sequence begins with tau(1)=1; for each later integer n it initializes count=2 and scans divisors from 2 through n-1, yielding the number of positive divisors. The zero-based term at index i is tau(i+1). The benchmark bounds indices to 0..9,999 to preserve the source scan with practical runtime; it is distinct from direct factorization-based number_of_positive_divisors.

The pinned Python djb2 processes each character code point as hash = hash*33 + code_point, then masks the final value to 32 bits. The benchmark bounds code points to 0..255 and input length to 0..64, returning the unsigned 32-bit result; it is distinct from the NUL-terminated, 64-bit C `hash_djb2` contract.

The pinned Python source validates uppercase A/T/C/G characters and uses a character translation map for the complementary DNA strand: A↔T and C↔G. The shared byte contract makes the alphabet and length bound explicit; this operation is separate from the T-to-U replacement in `dna2_rna` and the RNA complement in `rna_transcription`.

The pinned Julia source replaces every `T` with `U` and preserves all other characters. The shared byte contract accepts uppercase ASCII letters and caps the input at the source's documented 1,000-base length; unlike `rna_transcription`, it does not complement C/G or replace A.

Both pinned C++ dnf_sort files implement the same three-way partition for keys 0, 1, and 2 as dutch_national_flag_sort, so the candidate aliases that benchmark. The source dereferences size()-1 on empty input and has no default switch branch for other keys; those cases are outside its defined domain. The shared contract safely includes empty input and restricts keys to 0, 1, and 2.
The pinned Go paths are package documentation files containing comments only, not callable algorithms.

The pinned Python source provides separate positive-integer surface-area and volume formulas. The benchmark selects the two source functions with a selector and preserves their operation order on its bounded domain.

The pinned Python source uses Conway’s Doomsday rule, while the same-named Rust source uses fixed month offsets. The candidate maps to the Doomsday package and records the distinct Rust formula as an additional benchmark.

The pinned Python file exports `doppler_effect` and computes `(org_freq * (wave_vel + obs_vel)) / (wave_vel - src_vel)`, raising for equal wave/source speeds or nonpositive outputs. The benchmark bounds a positive subset that excludes both error cases and preserves the source expression order.

The pinned Python source implements a mutable linked deque class with append, pop, iteration, and observer methods. It is a stateful collection API rather than a single-call algorithm and is excluded from this benchmark catalog.

Inspected the pinned C++ sources in both C++ repositories, the C-Sharp BigInteger implementation, and the Python recursive and iterative forms. They compute the same-parity product with 0!! = 1; arbitrary-precision inputs and exception behavior vary. The shared scalar contract accepts 0 through 33, returns the exact signed 64-bit value, and returns -1 for negative inputs or values above 33.

The pinned TypeScript implementation uses iterative downward multiplication by two, matching the double_factorial algorithm. Its JavaScript Number result may round 31!! and 33!! because they exceed the exact integer range; 32!! remains exactly representable due its trailing powers of two. The i64 benchmark reports exact mathematical values through 33, so this mapping identifies the shared algorithm with that source precision caveat.

The pinned Python source subclasses mutable HashTable and supplies only a collision-resolution hook that depends on table size, probe increment, and inherited insertion state; it is a stateful container strategy rather than a standalone deterministic call.

Both pinned C++ sources are interactive demonstrations of open-addressed double hashing, distinct from linear and quadratic probing. They use global mutable state, diagnostic I/O, std::hash, resizing, and an uninitialized empty sentinel, so they are not directly callable benchmark functions. The shared bounded contract ports the double-hash strategy with deterministic integer hashes, prime capacities, explicit tombstones, and insert/search/delete operation streams. The separate Python double_hash candidate only overrides a mutable HashTable collision hook and is independently marked non-benchmarkable; it is not an equivalent standalone benchmark.

The pinned Python and Ruby sources probe the left endpoint before the right endpoint, then move inward. The contract preserves that duplicate-match order and bounds values to the JavaScript exact-integer range.

The pinned Python source checks the left position before the right position and recursively moves inward, returning the first index found or -1. For the default full-list invocation, its `right or len-1` fallback can repeat the center check at index zero but does not change the result; the bounded port preserves the observable left-then-right order over signed 32-bit integers.

The pinned MATLAB-Octave DoublePointCrossover draws a random permutation of positions, sorts its first two distinct cuts, keeps each parent's prefix through the first cut and suffix after the second cut, and exchanges the inclusive middle segment. The benchmark supplies those 1-based cut positions explicitly for deterministic calls and bounds genes to signed int32 values exactly representable by MATLAB numeric arrays. This remains distinct from uniform_crossover, which selects independently at every locus; this operator always exchanges one contiguous segment. All nine ports passed the byte-output verifier (141 oracle inputs and 13 workload records per language).
The pinned Python routine makes forward and backward adjacent-swap passes and produces the same ascending result as the canonical cocktail-sort benchmark.

The pinned Go Doubly type is a sentinel-based circular doubly linked list. AddAtBeg/AddAtEnd and DelAtBeg/DelAtEnd implement push and pop at both ends, while Front/Back expose the two end values (nil when empty). Those operations align with the linked_deque trace. Count, DelByPos, Reverse, and MoveToBack are additional list operations not covered by that shared deque contract; the node-pointer mutation methods are also outside its operation interface. This is an alias for the common end-operation subset, not a claim of full API equivalence.

The 14 pinned implementations share a doubly linked list structure, while their APIs vary across positional insertion/deletion, end operations, search, reversal, and size. The benchmark normalizes this family to append/prepend, pop at either end, remove the first matching value, contains, and length; its bounded index-based node pool is a portable benchmark representation.
The pinned C# source stores a generic payload and next/previous links; list operations are implemented elsewhere.

The pinned Python LinkedList uses a head/tail doubly linked structure. Its insert() appends, delete_value() unlinks the first matching node, __contains__ searches by value, and iteration traverses forward; these core list behaviors are represented by the canonical doubly_linked_list contract. insert_at_position() has a source-specific 1-based position with append-on-past-end behavior, and missing delete_value() raises; those details are outside the shared operation trace. The candidate is mapped to the canonical benchmark for its common linked-list operations.

The pinned Python source scrapes Google Images for a query and downloads matching image files into a local directory. It depends on live page structure and performs network and filesystem side effects, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.

The pinned Go package exposes deterministic DSA Verify alongside parameter/key generation and Sign. The bounded dsa_verify contract ports only the verification equation over small prime subgroups and big-endian messages; random crypto/rand parameter generation and nonce-based signing are excluded from deterministic benchmarking. Eight native ports passed the focused verifier; Elisa code generation emitted an unresolved dsa_verify_impl symbol at link time, so Elisa remains a source port but is not counted as passing.

The pinned C++ copies use recursive path compression and union by rank, while also tracking component size and minimum/maximum IDs. The shared partition trace ignores those extra statistics and representative shape, normalizes the source's one-based sample IDs, and uses only bounded valid indices. The source omits an explicit <algorithm> include for std::min/max/swap, so its include portability is not used as a property of the portable contract.

The pinned C++ copies implement disjoint-set union by rank without path compression and expose parent paths. They map to the shared partition trace after normalizing the source's one-based sample IDs; representative IDs and parent paths are ignored.

The pinned Python source seeds a dual number with coefficient 1 for epsilon, computes a power by repeated dual multiplication, then returns the selected epsilon coefficient times the derivative-order factorial (or the real value for order zero). The shared benchmark fixes the callable family to f(x)=x^p, bounds p and the derivative order to 0..8, and preserves the coefficient recurrence across nine portable ports.

The pinned Java source orders the first and final values as two pivots, partitions the range into lower, middle, and upper regions, and recursively sorts those regions. The shared benchmark retains the two-pivot partition, records explicit pivot boundaries, and recurses into the smaller partitions while iterating over the largest to bound stack depth.

The pinned Java predicate rejects nonpositive inputs, rounds a floating cube-root estimate, verifies the exact cube, and compares the root with the decimal digit sum. The benchmark preserves the positive-int predicate using exact integer cube-root search, avoiding floating-point rounding in all ports.

The pinned Java stack scan detects a parenthesis pair with no intervening expression content. This checks redundant grouping and remains separate from benchmarks that test whether parentheses are balanced.
The pinned PHP file only defines a LogicException subclass whose constructor formats a duplicate-key message and delegates to LogicException; it exposes no algorithmic operation.

The pinned C and C++ sources implement Durand–Kerner iteration for polynomial roots, but their command-line demos use random initialization and differ in update behavior. The benchmark defines a deterministic bounded cubic contract for x^3-d (nonzero integer d in [-4,4]), uses simultaneous updates from signed cube roots of unity, and returns selected root components through the i64_array_float64 ABI. It is distinct from the existing quadratic formula benchmark.
The pinned C++ source uses Duval's linear scan to select a lexicographically least cyclic rotation. This is distinct from the Rust `duval_algorithm` Lyndon-factorization operation.

The pinned Rust source performs Duval Lyndon factorization. The byte-output contract returns each factor length as a little-endian u32 word; this is distinct from the C++ `duval` minimal-cyclic-rotation algorithm.

The pinned C, Java, and Python sources share append, update-existing-index, get, and size operations. The contract defines the C initializer’s intended empty state, restricts Java put to existing indices, and fixes capacity at 16 because capacity is not observable in the shared API.

The pinned C# implementation is documented as a minimum-coin solver, but its executable rule builds remainders for each amount, then selects the remainder whose own remainder list has the smallest minimum; descending denomination order and strict comparisons retain the first tie. The output is the ordered selected-denomination sequence, not the minimum coin count (for coins [1,4,5] and amount 12 it returns [5,5,1,1]). The bounded adapter uses amounts 1..18 and unique denominations 1..9 including 1, with decimal digit concatenation for the returned sequence.
This Julia file is a module barrel that exports and includes a separate coin_change implementation; it contains no standalone algorithm body.

The pinned C# DynamicProgrammingKnapsackSolver builds a bottom-up 0/1 DP table and backtracks one optimal selected-item list. The existing knapsack_zero_one_tabulation contract computes the same maximum total value with the equivalent one-row descending-capacity recurrence. The benchmark observes optimal value rather than selected indices, so item-selection tie choices are intentionally normalized away. The alias applies to the shared contract domain (nonnegative capacity, positive integer weights, nonnegative integer values); source features outside that domain, including zero-weight items and arbitrary double-valued selectors, are not represented.

The pinned C source is an interactive dynamic-array stack implementation with push/pop/peek and console output. Its behavior is a sequence of stateful commands rather than one deterministic algorithm call, so it is excluded.

The pinned Java scalar distance(first, second, band) rejects empty or non-finite series and requires band >= abs(length difference). It uses a two-row dynamic program with previous[0]=0, +infinity elsewhere, and an inclusive 1-based Sakoe–Chiba range from max(1, i-band) to min(m, i+band). Each cell adds abs(first[i-1]-second[j-1]) to min(up, left, diagonal), returning the bottom-right cost. The benchmark uses bounded finite integer samples and does not include the separate path-returning overload.

The pinned Go tests construct a zero-value DynamicArray{}, giving capacity 0 until the first Add invokes NewCapacity and allocates 10 slots; later growth doubles. The source exposes Add, Put, Get, Remove, IsEmpty, GetData, and Capacity. The existing dynamic_array benchmark covers only the common append/update/get/size subset and uses a different unobservable capacity model. This separate contract adds stable removal, capacity and empty queries, and final GetData contents, so it is not a complete alias.

The pinned Python source repeatedly scans the live polygon for an ear, emits the previous/current/next vertices, removes the current vertex, and stops when no ear is found. It assumes valid simple polygons; the benchmark adds bounded integer geometry validation and deterministic index ordering. The C# `Triangulator` candidate computes station-position averages and is a different algorithm.

Both pinned C++ copies implement the same Gregorian computus and return a (0,0,0) sentinel through year 1582. The benchmark returns that sentinel as packed zero and bounds years to 0 through 9999, preserving the source operation with portable scalar results.

The pinned Java ECC demo randomly creates curve parameters but fixes its base point at (4, 8) without checking that it lies on the curve. Its message encoder similarly maps arbitrary values to (m, m), which is not generally a curve point, then applies group formulas that require valid curve points. The encryption/decryption example therefore does not implement valid elliptic-curve cryptography and has no deterministic portable key/input contract; excluded as an invalid implementation of its named algorithm.

The pinned Java scheduleProcesses() stably sorts processes by ascending deadline, then runs each process to completion while accumulating waiting and turnaround times. This is exactly the existing CPU-scheduling mode 3 (non-preemptive ascending-priority) when arrivals are all zero and priority values are the deadlines. The alias is restricted to the shared bounded positive-burst domain; the canonical contract reports per-process metrics in input order, which normalizes away the Java method's sorted returned-list order. The source's console warnings for missed deadlines are side effects and are not part of the returned schedule semantics.
This Go file defines the edge-node component of the Project Euler 18 triangle structure and delegates traversal/insertion as part of that composite model; it is not a standalone algorithm.

The pinned Go and Ruby editdistance sources implement ordinary unit-cost Levenshtein dynamic programming with insertion, deletion, and substitution. They map to the bounded ASCII levenshtein_distance contract; this candidate does not implement adjacent-transposition edits.

The pinned Go Edmond-Karp implementation has the same maximum-flow objective as the Java and TypeScript Edmonds–Karp sources; the spelling difference is treated as an upstream filename alias sharing the canonical bounded contract.

The pinned Java Edmonds.java source implements Chu–Liu/Edmonds minimum spanning arborescence for a directed weighted graph rooted at a supplied vertex. It is distinct from edmonds_blossom_algorithm, which computes maximum-cardinality matching in undirected general graphs, and edmonds_karp, which computes maximum flow. The shared contract bounds the graph to five vertices and twelve edges, uses nonnegative weights, and returns the minimum rooted arborescence cost or -1 when none exists. All nine language ports pass 259 oracle arrays and five workload records each.

The pinned Java and Python sources intend to find maximum-cardinality matchings in undirected general graphs by contracting odd-cycle blossoms during augmenting-path searches. This is distinct from Kuhn and Hopcroft–Karp, which require bipartite partitions. The pinned Python contract_blossom loops use a boolean expression as a range endpoint and do not traverse the intended paths; the shared bounded contract uses the standard O(V^3) Edmonds procedure, returns cardinality, accepts duplicate edges as one edge, and rejects self-loops and malformed packed input.

The pinned Java capacity-matrix and TypeScript adjacency-list sources both implement Edmonds–Karp maximum flow with breadth-first augmenting paths over residual capacities. The shared contract bounds integral capacities and excludes antiparallel input edges to keep TypeScript reverse-edge pairing unambiguous; all nine ports compare the maximum-flow value.

Despite its filename, the pinned Python source defines a PushRelabelExecutor and performs preflow/excess updates with relabel-to-front scheduling after adding super-source and super-sink vertices. Its constructor and executor disagree on camelCase versus snake_case field names, so the upstream file's current setup path is defective. The intended multi-terminal maximum-flow semantics share the canonical Push–Relabel contract.

The pinned Java, Python, and Rust sources share the bottom-up minimum-worst-case recurrence over first-drop floors. The contract restricts the domain to at least one egg and one floor, avoiding each source's unsupported zero-egg or zero-floor cases while preserving the results on the bounded range.

Both pinned C++ egg_dropping_puzzle copies implement the same eggs-by-floors minimax recurrence and first-drop search as the existing Java, Python, and Rust egg_dropping sources. The documented positive-egg and positive-floor domain is a subset of the canonical contract, so this source candidate aliases egg_dropping rather than defining another benchmark.

The pinned Go implementation uses the same bottom-up minimum worst-case recurrence over first-drop floors as the canonical Java, Python, and Rust candidate on the shared contract domain of at least one egg and one floor.

The pinned Java method repeatedly chooses x = ceil(denominator / numerator), appends the ordered term `1/x`, and updates numerator = numerator*x - denominator and denominator = denominator*x until numerator is zero. The bounded contract uses exact integer arithmetic and encodes the same ordered unit-fraction denominators as little-endian i32 values; all nine ports and the rational oracle were statically reviewed.

The pinned Java class combines secure random safe-prime key generation (minimum modulus size 256 bits), randomized encryption with an internally sampled ephemeral exponent k, and BigInteger decryption. The signed-i64 benchmark ABI cannot represent the documented key sizes, and ciphertext output is nondeterministic because the source does not accept k or a random source as input. The encrypt/decrypt math is related to Diffie–Hellman modular exponentiation but is not equivalent to the existing shared-secret contract; mapping it would misrepresent the API. Excluded from deterministic portable benchmarking.

The pinned Java resolveCollision computes the center normal and relative velocity, leaves the first body unchanged when centers overlap or bodies move apart, and otherwise applies an elastic impulse with restitution 1. The bounded contract supplies two bodies as twelve fixed-thousandths integers, excludes coincident centers, and packs the first body’s rounded post-collision velocity components into signed 16-bit x/y words in an i64 result. The source impulse is still applied at exact tangency and, as written, to separated bodies when they are approaching.

The pinned Python function requires exactly one zero, rejects negative inputs, uses electron charge 1.6021e-19, and follows the documented three formula branches. The benchmark maps it to the integer domain 1..1000 for each nonzero input; all nine ports and workload follow that bounded subset and use -1e300 for invalid inputs.

The pinned Python function requires exactly one of voltage, current, and power to be zero, rejects negative power, and solves the missing value using P=VI. It preserves signs in the voltage/current division branches and rounds absolute voltage-times-current to two decimals for the power branch; the integer-valued bounded benchmark domain makes that rounding an identity.

The pinned Python function requires exactly one zero and solves the missing component with sqrt(Z²-X²), sqrt(Z²-R²), or sqrt(R²+X²). The benchmark preserves these branches on a bounded nonnegative integer domain, maps negative radicands and other invalid inputs to -1e300, and measures the numeric result rather than the source name/value pair.

The pinned JavaScript function computes one generation from an arbitrary elementary rule. The benchmark fixes rule 30 and requires the first cell to be zero, which avoids the pinned source’s left-neighbor indexing discrepancy at cell index 1. It matches the pinned Python rule_30_step semantics on this bounded domain; all nine target-language ports implement the same finite-row evolution.
The pinned Python source implements Rule 30 only; its rule_30_step is equivalent to the JavaScript canonical benchmark on the restricted contract with first cell zero.

The pinned Python source applies the ELF high-nibble fold with unbounded integers. The bounded ASCII contract preserves bit 32 for seven 15-codepoints followed by 16 and rejects inputs longer than eight codepoints.

The pinned Python generate_key routine generates a random large prime, chooses random values, prints progress, and make_key_files writes public/private key files. Its 2048-bit default is outside the signed-i64 ABI; randomness and filesystem/output side effects prevent a deterministic single-call contract. Its primitive_root helper also does not check true primitivity: for prime p, pow(g, p, p) equals g, so it mainly rejects g=1 (along with squares equal to 1). It is key setup, not the Java cipher operation and not equivalent to the existing deterministic primitive_root or Diffie–Hellman benchmarks. Excluded from portable benchmarking.

The pinned Rust source implements affine elliptic-curve points and their group addition, negation, and subtraction over prime fields. The existing elliptic_curve_key_exchange benchmark already ports and exercises the same affine addition law in all nine languages as the core of its bounded scalar-multiplication/ECDH contract, so this filename is cataloged as covered by that benchmark.

The two pinned C++ files implement affine point addition and binary double-and-add for an ECDH demo; the additional repository copy agrees on these operations. The benchmark standardizes that flow over validated small prime fields, computes both public points and the shared point in both directions, and emits three little-endian point pairs. It excludes the demo’s fixed large parameters, custom 128/256-bit arithmetic tests, and console output; the bounded benchmark makes no cryptographic-security claim.

The pinned MATLAB-Octave file is an interactive plotting demo, but its displayed activation expression is a deterministic ELU: alpha * (exp(x) - 1) for x < 0 and x for x > 0, with zero at x == 0. The new scalar benchmark isolates that formula, supplies alpha explicitly, and applies a bounded finite binary64 domain. It is distinct from exponential_linear_unit, whose pinned Rust expression differs on negative inputs.

The pinned Java EMAFilter accepts finite alpha values in (0, 1], returns an empty trace for an empty input, seeds each nonempty apply call from its first sample, and then updates as alpha * current + (1 - alpha) * previous EMA. The benchmark uses alpha=k/1024 and at most four samples, so there are at most three updates; bounded integer samples keep the exact rational numerator below 2^53, matching byte-for-byte binary64 output across the ports.

The pinned Python source fetches a user-supplied site, follows links, and extracts addresses from live page contents. Results vary with external websites and network state, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.
The pinned Java file only defines a checked exception with message and message-plus-cause constructors; it delegates to Exception and exposes no algorithmic operation.

Both pinned Java methods reverse the four bytes of a signed 32-bit integer. The benchmark preserves Java int32 signed interpretation through the i64 ABI, and maps values outside the Java input range to the documented sentinel.

The pinned Python module exposes swap_endianness_16/32/64, bytes_to_int_little/big, and int_to_bytes_little/big. The nine-port contract covers all seven operations, bounds byte conversion lengths to 1..8, and transports UInt64 values/results as signed i64 bit patterns. It is distinct from endian_converter, which reverses signed 32-bit values, and byte_encoding_utils, which has a narrower unsigned byte-encoding contract.

The pinned Rust convert_energy function converts the input to joules using the selected source-unit factor, then divides by the selected target-unit factor. The shared contract preserves all 55 enum factors and this multiplication-then-division order on a bounded finite input domain.

The pinned Python source checks the selected unit names and computes `value * ENERGY_CONVERSION[from_type] / ENERGY_CONVERSION[to_type]` in that order. The benchmark preserves the 13 source units and exact factor constants through a numeric-code adapter, bounds finite inputs, and defines an explicit malformed-input sentinel.

The pinned Python source uses a 94-character printable-ASCII alphabet, identity rotors, and a reversed reflector, but stores rotor positions and the output list in module-global mutable state. encode_or_decode advances those globals before processing and never resets or clears them, so output and subsequent calls depend on prior runtime history; menu() also performs interactive I/O. This is not equivalent to enigma_machine2's local-state uppercase rotor core and is excluded as stateful/non-deterministic for a repeatable single-call benchmark.

The pinned Python implementation uses a 26-letter uppercase alphabet, three selectable permutation rotors, a reciprocal A↔N..M↔Z reflector, optional plugboard, and local per-call rotor positions. This benchmark selects the source's default three rotors, empty plugboard, and uppercase letter inputs; it preserves its 1-based initial positions and simple carry stepping (no notch turnover), with at most 12 letters encoded as a base-26 scalar. The sibling enigma_machine.py uses 94 printable ASCII symbols and persistent global mutable state, so it is not an alias. All nine ports pass 270 oracle arrays and five workload records.

The pinned Python source counts all ASCII characters and adjacent bigrams in the denominators, but only space and lowercase a-z in the entropy sums. It rounds each raw entropy or conditional difference with Python's ties-to-even integer `round()` before one-decimal formatting. The byte-output contract returns the exact three newline-terminated lines and reports the actual output byte length, which can be 13.
The pinned C# file is a generic mutable key/value holder used by a hash table; it has no standalone algorithmic behavior.
The pinned MATLAB file is a beginner tutorial demonstrating assignment (`a = 3; b = a`) and printing the value; it implements no algorithm function.
The pinned MATLAB file is a beginner tutorial demonstrating assignment and increment (`a = a + 1`) and printing the value; it implements no algorithm function.

The pinned Python class cascades a 10th-order Yule–Walker filter with a 150 Hz Butterworth high-pass at 44,100 Hz, with per-call zeroed histories. The source designs Yule–Walker coefficients at runtime using loudness-curve data, FFT, least-squares solves, and root stabilization. The portable benchmark fixes the generated coefficients in signed Q30 and defines truncation-toward-zero integer recurrence on scaled bounded traces; this is an explicit fixed-coefficient profile, not runtime coefficient-design parity. It is distinct from the individual Butterworth coefficient benchmark and general IIR recurrence.

The pinned Python and Rust sources compute the monthly payment from principal, annual decimal rate, and integral years using r=rate/12, n=years*12, and p*r*(1+r)^n/((1+r)^n-1). The package uses the shared positive-rate domain and bounded inputs, preserves the formula, and documents the upstream zero-rate/API differences. The float64_triple recorder now validates this algorithm and its expected formula.

The pinned Python source computes the total once, scans from left to right, subtracts the current value before comparing left and right sums, and returns the first matching index or -1. The packed i32 input bound keeps the accumulation safely within i64.

The pinned C++ source marks composite multiples in a boolean sieve, the same Sieve of Eratosthenes recurrence as the canonical candidate. The shared contract reports the prime count through an inclusive limit; inputs below 2 are handled by the adapter because the source directly indexes sieve entries 0 and 1.
The pinned PHP source intends the same Sieve of Eratosthenes, but leaves 1 in its returned array. The shared contract uses corrected sieve semantics and counts primes from 2.

The pinned Python erosion function multiplies a binary image window by the supplied kernel and writes one exactly when the sum is 5. The shared contract uses the source demo’s 3x3 cross kernel and zero padding; its grayscale conversion and file-based image demo are outside this operation contract.

The pinned Python source computes sqrt(2*G*mass/radius) in that order and rounds the resulting binary64 to 3 decimal places. The ports use a fused residual against the half-thousand midpoint to reproduce Python rounding; the workload includes mass=825929310938975, radius=1e9, where scale-first rounding would return 0.01 but Python returns 0.011. The bounded domain preserves zero mass and excludes invalid negative mass/zero radius.

The pinned Fortran module uses the iterative Euclidean remainder recurrence after taking absolute values. Its default integer type is narrower than the benchmark ABI; on representable nonnegative integer inputs it computes the same GCD as the shared `gcd` contract.

The pinned C# sequence is primorial(n)+1: zero-based index 0 returns 2, then 3, 7, 31, and so on. The nine ports preserve the +1 offset and bound indices to 0..15 so all results fit signed i64; later terms overflow the ABI.

The pinned C# Euclidean.Distance method computes the same N-dimensional square-root-of-squared-differences formula as the shared euclidean_distance contract; the benchmark normalizes double-array inputs to bounded integer coordinate arrays.

The pinned C implementation swaps a and b when |a|<|b| but does not swap the returned coefficients back. For positive input (99,303), its own expected coefficients (-16,49) satisfy 303*(-16)+99*49=3 rather than 99*(-16)+303*49=3. It therefore violates the existing full-order Bezout contract when a<b; only the restricted subdomain a>=b is coherent, so this source is excluded from that shared contract.

The pinned JavaScript, MATLAB-Octave, Python, R, and Rust sources compute the n-dimensional Euclidean distance as the square root of the sum of squared coordinate differences. Their behavior for vectors with unequal lengths differs; the shared benchmark contract requires an explicit dimension and exact input length, uses an invalid sentinel for malformed data, and preserves the shared mathematical formula.

The pinned Ruby function repeatedly replaces `(a, b)` with `(b, a % b)` and returns `a`. For nonnegative integer inputs this is the same GCD operation; its arbitrary-precision and negative-input behavior are outside the shared benchmark representation.

The pinned C# finder uses iterative Euclid for positive integers, but returns `int.MaxValue` for `(0, 0)` and has nonstandard negative-input behavior. Its positive integer domain matches the shared `gcd` operation; the benchmark’s zero convention is separately defined.

The pinned Zig function recursively applies modulo and is generic over integer and floating-point types. This alias covers its integer GCD operation on nonnegative inputs; the benchmark contract uses bounded unsigned integer words and defines `(0, 0) -> 0`.

The pinned C program wraps a helper that checks only Euler-trail endpoint degree parity; it does not test connectivity. The benchmark isolates and faithfully ports that helper over a bounded simple undirected graph input, preserving the parity-only behavior.

The pinned C#, Java, JavaScript, and Python sources share forward Euler updates for y' = x+y. The package uses a binary-exact dyadic grid and normalizes output to the y trajectory; Julia uses a distinct span/time API, floor step count, and state/time vector behavior, tracked as `euler_method_julia`.

The pinned Jupyter notebook is an interactive demonstration with a function that mutates global Xlist/Ylist and prints a table, plus a globally defined example derivative and plotting-oriented workflow. The algorithm is standard forward Euler but the notebook does not expose a standalone benchmark entrypoint.

The pinned Python function uses the explicit trapezoid (Heun) predictor-corrector update: an Euler predictor followed by averaging the two endpoint derivatives. The bounded benchmark uses the source docstring example ODE y'=-2xy^2 with x0=0 and h=0.25, returning the full trajectory. This is distinct from the existing explicit midpoint method.

The pinned Java isProbablePrime method uses one static mutable Random seeded with 1. Calls advance shared PRNG state, so an odd composite can be accepted for one set of bases and rejected for another; the same input and trial count can therefore depend on call order across recorder repetitions. A stateless per-call oracle cannot represent this method under the repeatable-call ABI without modeling or resetting the shared RNG stream. The public jacobiSymbol helper is deterministic, but benchmarking it would be a different algorithm contract.

The pinned Rust and TypeScript sources compute the scalar Euler totient by factorizing n and applying the prime-factor product formula. The benchmark bounds positive n to 1..1,000,000 and returns -1 outside that domain.

The pinned C-Sharp sequence emits phi(1), phi(2), and so on; it factors each integer independently and applies the distinct-prime formula. The benchmark bounds the prefix at 80 and preserves that repeated-factorization approach.

The pinned Rust module applies directed degree-balance conditions, selects the unique +1 vertex or the lowest vertex with outgoing edges, then uses recursive Hierholzer traversal while consuming each adjacency list from the end. It returns no path for empty-edge graphs or when degree constraints or full-edge traversal fail. The portable contract adds explicit bounds for vertices, edge count, and endpoints; it accepts parallel edges and self-loops and uses iterative Hierholzer traversal with the same edge order.

The pinned Python source classifies undirected Euler paths by odd-degree count and has a DFS helper that can return a trail. The shared domain is a simple undirected graph connected across all nonzero-degree vertices, with no self-loops or parallel edges, labels in the source's range, and vertex 1 present for circuit cases. It preserves input adjacency order and starts a circuit at vertex 1; a two-odd-vertex path starts at the highest odd label. The source does not check connectivity and collapses parallel edges, so those cases are excluded. Its printed wrapper is outside the contract.
The pinned Java source computes Euler’s totient by prime factorization and the standard product update, matching `euler_totient` on the shared positive bounded domain.

The pinned Dart, JavaScript, and Julia sources compute scalar phi(n) by the distinct-prime formula; Python returns phi(1)..phi(n) with a linear sieve. The Python implementation has an incorrect phi[1] initialization and includes an invalid boundary update, so its sequence is ported to a separately bounded linear-sieve benchmark with corrected conventional recurrence.
The pinned C++ and JavaScript sources implement the scalar Euler totient with prime factorization and the distinct-prime product formula. They share the bounded phi(n) contract.
The pinned Go Phi function factors the reduced input and applies the distinct-prime product formula, matching the scalar Euler totient contract.

The pinned JavaScript evaluatePostfixExpression consumes whitespace-separated reverse Polish notation from left to right, pushing parsed numeric operands and applying +, -, *, and / with the right operand popped first. The existing benchmark preserves the stack order and source null behavior for underflow, unknown operators, division by zero, and leftover values, while using a bounded milli-unit numeric encoding instead of locale-sensitive strings. It is distinct from postfix_evaluation integer truncation and postfix_evaluator Java int32 wrapping.

The pinned Python source roots the tree at node 1, computes subtree sizes, and counts edges whose child subtree has even size. The benchmark requires a valid tree with an even number of nodes and preserves the source's cut-count result.

The pinned Solidity contract demonstrates event emission in a payable state-changing transaction. Its observable result depends on caller/value and chain event state, not a deterministic algorithm call.

The pinned Java and Python sources both classify a nonnegative integer as evil when the number of set bits in its binary representation is even; both classify zero as evil. The contract normalizes Java’s original signed-int bound and Python’s arbitrary-precision inputs to portable nonnegative signed-64-bit values, returning 1/0 and -1 for negatives. This returns parity, distinct from `hamming_weight`, which returns the count.

The pinned Java detector smooths samples around a target with an EWMA, tests a warm-up-dependent control limit, emits directional alarms, and resets its average to target after each alarm. This differs from EMAFilter, which only returns a smoothed trace, and from robust local outlier filters. The portable profile fixes target=0, sigma=1, alpha=1/2, width=1 and bounds integer samples to [-8,8] for at most 15 steps. It uses an exact rational EWMA numerator and squared control-limit comparison (3*d^2 > 4^n-1), with reset after alarms, and base-4 packs the signal trace.

The pinned Python function rejects empty strings and nonalphabetic input, uppercases the title, then scans right to left, adding (A=1..Z=26) times successive powers of 26. The benchmark preserves that base-26 conversion over bounded ASCII letters; Unicode alphabetic characters are outside the shared contract.

The pinned Python function clamps negative inputs to zero, scans the resulting decimal digits, adds three to each digit, and appends each four-bit nibble after the literal `0b` prefix. The shared contract accepts the full signed-64-bit input range and writes ASCII to a caller buffer. All nine ports passed an independent per-digit oracle, including signed boundaries and insufficient output capacities.

The pinned C-Sharp implementation compares every pair (i,j) with j>i and swaps when the pair is inverted, matching exchange_sort. Its XML summary calls it stable, but pairwise exchanges do not generally preserve equal-key order.
The pinned Go implementation compares each position with every later position and swaps out-of-order pairs, matching exchange_sort.
The PHP class records microtime in its constructor/destructor and prints elapsed time; it is a profiling helper, not an algorithm.

The pinned Python historical-simulation source sorts returns, linearly interpolates the empirical quantile at 1-confidence, includes all values at or below that threshold in the tail, and returns the negative tail mean. The bounded contract preserves those choices and rejects empty inputs or invalid confidence with the sentinel.

The pinned C++ source provides exponential-rate expected value, variance, and standard deviation (1/lambda, 1/lambda^2, and 1/lambda) and rejects nonpositive lambda. The bounded contract exposes those three operations with a positive finite rate and invalid-input sentinel.
The pinned JavaScript source computes a bounded, truncated Taylor sum for e^x with a source-specific zero-term special case. It is not a call to the platform exponential function.

The pinned Rust function returns x for x >= 0 and computes x * (alpha * (exp(x) - 1)) for x < 0 in that operation order. The pinned Python sibling differs for negative x; the package follows Rust source behavior.

Pinned Python and Rust sources share the batch EMA warm-up and recurrence only on `window_size >= 2`; the package preserves their source update order over integer prices. Java is a different streaming state API that applies the standard one-step EWMA immediately and is tracked as the additional `exponential_moving_average_java_stream` package.

The inspected sources implement exponential range expansion followed by a search in the bounded region, with varying element widths, APIs, and search details. The local benchmark standardizes ascending signed 64-bit input and returns any matching index, or -1 when absent.
The Solidity source stores two uint16 values and returns their checked, unmodded power. The bounded contract keeps base^exponent within signed 64-bit output and avoids uint256 overflow.

Despite the filename and helper variables, the pinned Ruby function returns only the Euclidean gcd; it computes a coefficient internally but does not return a Bezout tuple. Its nonnegative integer behavior, including zero inputs, matches the existing gcd benchmark contract.

The pinned Go recursive source returns (gcd,x,y) from the standard extended-Euclid recurrence. On positive signed-i32 inputs it satisfies a*x+b*y=gcd and fits the existing extended_euclidean_algorithm contract; the shared contract excludes zero and negative inputs.

The pinned C++ iterative and recursive implementations swap A and B to order them but do not swap the returned coefficients back. For positive inputs with A<B, the returned x,y correspond to the reordered pair rather than the original arguments. This violates the existing full-order Bezout contract, so the source is excluded from that shared contract.

Inspected the pinned C-Sharp, Java, Python, R, and Rust sources. C-Sharp returns the two Bezout coefficients before the GCD in its result record; Java and Rust return (gcd,x,y); Python returns only the coefficients; and R includes recursive, iterative, modular-inverse, and Diophantine helpers. Their sign and zero-input behavior differs. The shared benchmark restricts inputs to two positive signed-32-bit integers and returns (gcd,x,y), satisfying a*x+b*y=gcd. The output is three signed 32-bit two's-complement values in little-endian byte order. The nine portable ports use iterative Euclid with checked coefficient bounds.

The pinned JavaScript source validates positive numeric arguments, reorders them recursively when needed, and swaps the returned Bezout coefficients back to the original argument order. On positive signed-i32 inputs its Number arithmetic is exact and it returns (gcd,x,y) satisfying a*x+b*y=gcd, matching the existing extended_euclidean_algorithm contract.

The pinned Nim source computes gcd and Bezout coefficients with iterative Euclid, then applies each input sign to its corresponding coefficient. On the shared positive signed-i32 domain it returns (gcd,x,y) satisfying a*x+b*y=gcd and matches the existing extended_euclidean_algorithm contract.

The pinned Java ExtendedKalmanFilter is a vector-state EKF with nonlinear transition and measurement callbacks, Jacobians evaluated at the current estimate, and Joseph-form covariance correction. It is distinct from the scalar KalmanFilter candidate/contract: no existing local Kalman benchmark covers these equations. The bounded extended_kalman_filter trace fixes a 2-state quadratic transition and scalar quadratic observation. C, C++, Rust, Zig, C3, Nim, Odin, and V passed the focused verifier (17 oracle arrays and 7 workload cases each). Elisa is present as a direct native source translation but stage1 emitted no exported symbol; the direct-export backend limitation is reproduced in benchmarks/elisa_stage1_export_probe/README.md and Elisa is not counted as verified.
The pinned Go iterative implementation matches the extended Euclidean benchmark for positive int32 inputs; its source assumes a > 0.

The pinned Go iterative source returns (gcd,x,y) from Euclid's quotient recurrence. On positive signed-i32 inputs it satisfies a*x+b*y=gcd and fits the existing extended_euclidean_algorithm contract; zero and negative behavior are outside the shared positive-input domain.

The pinned C# class exposes FlattenTree and RebuildFromList helpers that convert a scapegoat tree subtree to an inorder node list and rebuild it around midpoint nodes. ScapegoatTree.cs invokes both only as part of its insertion/deletion rebalancing; the file does not define an independent data structure or general-purpose algorithm contract. These helpers belong to the separate scapegoat_tree candidate and are excluded as a standalone candidate.

The pinned C# implementation performs bottom-up merge passes over sequential storage, beginning with run width 1 and doubling the width while swapping source and temporary stores. The benchmark models those passes with two bounded buffers and returns the sorted signed 64-bit values; actual disk I/O and storage adapters are excluded.

The pinned Python NWayMerge.select initializes min_str to None but never updates it while scanning choices. The condition therefore remains true for every run head and returns the last index rather than the smallest head, so the merge step does not produce sorted output in general. Excluded as an invalid external-sort implementation.

The pinned Jupyter notebook downloads the AT&T face-image dataset from Google Drive, reads images with OpenCV, and trains/evaluates an eigenfaces recognizer using NumPy linear algebra. The measured result depends on a large external image corpus and numerical-library eigenvector behavior, so this notebook is a dataset-driven ML workflow rather than a bounded deterministic benchmark function.

The inspected C source prints arbitrary-precision decimal digits, and C++ uses recursion with an input limit of 20. The local scalar contract uses an iterative signed 64-bit product for inputs 0 through 20 and returns -1 outside that range.

The pinned Dart source evaluates Ramanujan's factorial approximation sqrt(pi)*(x/e)^x*(8*x^3+4*x^2+x+1/30)^(1/6) with the same operation order used by all nine ports. It does not validate inputs; the benchmark specifies finite x in [0,170], preserving the source's approximate value at zero rather than substituting exact 0!.

The pinned C program stores decimal digits least-significant first and multiplies by every factor from 2 through n, then prints the digits in reverse. The benchmark exposes this core base-10 digit-array computation for n in 0..100 and returns decimal bytes without the source program's interactive prompt or timing output.

The pinned C++ source seeds a memo vector with 1 and recursively caches n*f(n-1). It returns the same exact factorial for the shared valid range 0..20; 20! fits both uint64 and signed i64. The source explicitly does not handle overflow and its uint64_t input makes negative ABI inputs unsafe, so the shared contract range-checks and returns -1 outside 0..20.
The pinned Ruby routine uses a non-recursive, non-iterative product strategy and formats its result; after projecting the numeric result, it matches factorial for 0..20.

The pinned Dart and Java sources implement the same recursive factorial recurrence with 0! = 1 and 1! = 1. They return the exact shared results for n=0..20; 20! fits signed i64 and is exactly representable by Dart integer implementations. Invalid inputs are outside the source-compatible valid range: Java throws for negatives, Dart has no negative guard, and the benchmark returns -1 outside 0..20.

The pinned C# sequence yields 0!, 1!, 2!, ... using BigInteger and an incremental recurrence. The existing factorial benchmark computes the same term on the shared 0..20 signed-i64-safe domain. This alias identifies the same sequence values; the C# source is a lazy generator while the benchmark performs a per-call factorial loop.

The pinned C source sums n divided by successive powers of five, counting factors of five in n!, which determines its decimal trailing-zero count. The benchmark uses repeated integer division and accepts 0 through 1,000,000,000, returning -1 outside that range. All nine ports passed 10,545 oracle inputs per language and 16 workload cases.

The pinned Lua function returns a table mapping prime factors to multiplicities. Its tested edge behavior is `{[0] = 1}` for zero and `{[1] = 1}` for one; positive inputs greater than one use trial division through the square root. The bounded contract preserves the zero and one singleton mappings and serializes sorted (factor, exponent) pairs as little-endian u32 values for inputs 0 through 1,000,005. The nine portable ports use an integer division bound.

Inspected the pinned Dart, JavaScript, Python, Rust, and TypeScript sources. They enumerate positive divisors but differ on nonpositive values, traversal strategy, and result ordering: Dart scans upward from one, JavaScript includes zero in its candidate sequence, Python and Rust search divisor pairs through the square root and sort, and TypeScript inserts divisor pairs into a Set. The shared contract accepts 1 through 256, returns every positive divisor once in ascending order as comma-separated ASCII bytes, returns -1 for out-of-range input, and returns -2 without writing when output capacity is insufficient. The nine portable ports use integer trial division.

The Java source aggregates task weights for each named user, divides each user weight by the total weight, multiplies by total resources, and casts to int. It assigns each user independently, so fractional resource remainders are not distributed. The shared contract bounds total aggregate weight to prevent Java int overflow, ignores tasks for unknown user IDs as addTask does, maps zero total weight to zero allocations (Java casts NaN to zero), and sorts output IDs for determinism.

The pinned MATLAB implementation uses the bracket-preserving regula-falsi update for f(a)<0 and f(b)>0. The mirrored C++ helpers interpolate but always recurse on the previous second endpoint and the new point without preserving the sign-changing bracket; the default x^2-x scan with a 0.5 step lands exactly on roots 0 and 1 and does not exercise that helper. The shared benchmark follows the intended bracket-preserving method, standardizes the callback to x^2-x, isolates one root with bounded endpoints, and returns -1 for invalid pairs.

The pinned Python function computes `round(-(final_flux - initial_flux) / time_interval, 1)` and raises for negative time intervals; zero reaches division by zero. The portable contract uses milliweber and millisecond integer inputs, returns decivolts, and defines exact ties-to-even rounding with bounded integer arithmetic. It excludes zero intervals and maps invalid cases to the signed-64 minimum sentinel.

The pinned JavaScript source repeatedly updates lower and upper Farey bounds by mediants and returns the final mediant. The benchmark uses integer millionths for the target and preserves the source comparison/tie direction.

The pinned Java implementation takes base, exponent, and modulus and uses modular exponentiation by squaring, so it maps to `modular_exponentiation` on the shared positive-modulus domain. The pinned PHP implementation takes base and exponent and computes the unmodded power by squaring; it is recorded separately as `binary_exponentiation` when the exact result fits its bounded output domain.

The pinned Rust source uses a sieve, Legendre prime exponents, binary exponent buckets, and a balanced powers-by-squaring product. The benchmark limits n to 0..20 for exact signed-i64 output; out-of-range inputs return -1. This is algorithmically distinct from iterative factorial.

The pinned Python fast-doubling function returns F(n) using the recursive pair (F(n), F(n+1)); it matches the shared fast Fibonacci benchmark exactly for indices 0..92. Arbitrary-precision results beyond the signed-64-bit benchmark domain are excluded.
The pinned JavaScript function uses recursive fast doubling and returns F(n). It matches fibonacci_fast on indices 0..92; negative inputs are outside the shared domain.

The pinned C++ and Rust sources implement the same forward radix-2 DFT with positive-angle twiddles; C++ uses recursion and Rust uses iterative butterflies with bit reversal. The package accepts power-of-two real integer samples and returns interleaved fixed-point complex bins.
The pinned C++ source is a stdin parsing helper with a demo `main`, not a computational algorithm with a stable data-in/data-out workload.

The pinned Python implementation matches `fast_inverse_square_root` on positive finite inputs. Go uses a distinct binary32 magic-seed approximation with two Newton corrections and maps to `fast_inverse_sqrt_go`. Java returns exact-equality checks rather than approximation values; its float and double overloads are mapped to `fast_inverse_sqrt_java_check` using mode 0 or 1 and positive normal raw IEEE input bits. The Go benchmark pins explicit binary32 rounding after each intermediate operation; Go permits floating-point fusion across expressions, so exact bit-level results may vary by compiler and target.

The pinned PHP source narrows input to IEEE-754 binary32, reinterprets the bits with the 0x5f3759df magic constant and signed right shift, then performs one Newton correction using the original binary64 input. The benchmark preserves that approximate result, restricts input to a positive finite binary32-safe range, and uses portable language bit reinterpretations or arithmetic decoding rather than an architecture-specific reciprocal-square-root instruction.

The pinned Rust function computes base^power modulo a positive modulus and aliases modular_exponentiation. The C++ sources expose recursive and iterative nonmodular exponentiation for signed exponents; these map to powx_n. The filename candidate therefore has two distinct benchmark contracts.

The pinned C# FastSearcher combines an interpolation estimate with a binary midpoint, selects the segment that may contain the target, and recursively searches that segment. The shared contract preserves this hybrid probe strategy on a strictly increasing, bounded integer array; its bounds keep source 32-bit interpolation arithmetic safe, and missing-target exceptions map to -1.

The pinned Python module provides XOR, OR, and AND Walsh-Hadamard transforms and related convolutions. The benchmark covers its forward and inverse XOR transform as the core bounded operation; it keeps n to positive powers of two through 128 and bounds values so signed 64-bit butterfly arithmetic is safe.

The pinned Rust generator enumerates primes up to its logarithmic bound, applies the Lucas–Lehmer test to Mersenne numbers, forms each Euclid–Euler perfect number, and filters by the input limit. The package preserves this enumeration on a range that keeps the source's `num * 8 + 1` usize intermediate safe and emits ascending i64 values.

The pinned Go file provides iterative and recursive unmodded exponentiation variants. They compute the same exact integer power as `binary_exponentiation` when the exponent is nonnegative and the result fits the shared output domain.

The Julia function accepts process IDs and burst times in an already chosen FCFS order, then computes cumulative waiting and turnaround times and their averages. This is the same prefix-sum scheduling calculation represented by `fcfs_scheduling` when processes are already ordered and all are available before execution; zero-process behavior is outside the alias domain.

The two pinned C++ files are mirrored non-preemptive FCFS schedulers. Processes run in ascending arrival-time order; equal arrivals use ascending process ID, and the CPU idles until the next arrival. The self-test/demo output is excluded from timing. The bounded shared contract requires unique IDs and reports completion, turnaround, and waiting times for each scheduled process.

The pinned Java scheduler consumes its `ProcessDetails` list in the supplied order, assigns each waiting time from prior burst durations, and sets turnaround time to waiting plus burst. It aliases the ordered, no-idle subset of `fcfs_scheduling`; arrival-time sorting and empty output are handled by the shared benchmark contract.

The pinned Python federated_average normalizes nonnegative client weights by their positive sum and uses them to aggregate each client tensor coordinate. The portable contract scopes this operation to one scalar tensor per client, explicit weights, and bounded integer inputs represented exactly as float64 values; NumPy tensor-shape and optional equal-weight handling are outside this shared contract.

The pinned C# source is a concrete 32-round, 64-bit toy Feistel cipher, distinct from standard DES and not a configurable generic network. Its Math.Pow(double)-to-uint round-key schedule has no 32-round key domain with defined portable semantics: key 1 produces a zero round key and keys >=2 exceed uint range during the schedule. The mapped feistel_cipher_normalized benchmark is explicitly a normalized variant, not exact source parity: it defines round keys as wrapping_pow_u32(key, round+2) XOR key and all arithmetic modulo 2^32, preserving the source's 32-step arithmetic F-function and 32 outer Feistel rounds. Keys whose normalized round keys are zero are invalid to avoid division by zero. Source ASCII block zero-padding and NUL-stripping are documented; the contract tests one raw 64-bit block so the cipher core remains reversible.

Reviewed all seven pinned Fenwick-tree sources in C++ (two repositories), Java, JavaScript, Julia, Python, and Rust. They share point-add updates and prefix or range sums but differ in public indexing and whether ranges are inclusive or half-open. The shared contract standardizes zero-based point additions and inclusive range sums, with a bounded signed-64-bit workload.

The pinned Go source builds a one-based Fenwick tree, applies point-add updates, and answers inclusive range sums by subtracting prefix sums. These operations match the canonical Fenwick-tree contract after normalizing public indices to zero-based array positions and applying its bounded trace domain.

The pinned Python implementation uses modular exponentiation by squaring. It shares `modular_exponentiation` on the common positive-modulus domain; its special exponent-zero result is excluded when modulus is one.
The pinned C-Sharp sequence repeatedly squares 2 to emit 2^(2^n)+1. The bounded scalar contract includes indices 0 through 5, the largest term that fits signed 64-bit output.

The pinned C# checker seeds System.Random with default(DateTime).Millisecond, always zero, and starts its loop counter at one, so it performs timesToCheck - 1 Fermat checks. The bounded contract preserves the legacy seeded Random(0) stream, excludes the vacuous-check domain, and returns a probable-prime result rather than a primality proof.

The pinned C# `FermatPrimesSequence` takes the first five outputs of `FermatNumbersSequence` unchanged. It therefore matches terms F(0)..F(4) of the existing bounded Fermat-number benchmark; the name is historical and does not filter for primality.

The pinned Dart file is marked `@Skip('currently failing')` and is not valid Dart: the annotation precedes imports, and the recursive branch assigns the result of integer division `/` (a double) to an `int`. It is excluded as an invalid source rather than mapped to the Python implementation.

The pinned Python source scrapes a third-party anime site for search results, episodes, and media playlist URLs. Its results depend on live page structure and external media state, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.

The pinned Python source calls NewsAPI and prints the current BBC article titles. Its result depends on API credentials, live news data, and service availability, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.

The pinned Python source calls GitHub’s authenticated-user API using an access token and returns provider account data. It depends on credentials and external service state, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.
The pinned Python source scrapes current Indeed job listings by location. Results depend on live website contents and page structure, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.
The pinned Python source fetches daily or random quotes from the ZenQuotes API. Results depend on live external API data and availability, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.

The pinned Python source scrapes current prescription prices by drug name and ZIP code from WellRx. Results depend on live location-specific data and page structure, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.

The pinned Java FFT uses iterative radix-2 Cooley–Tukey with bit reversal and zero-pads to the next power of two. It implements the same transform family as the existing `fast_fourier_transform` benchmark; this maps its forward operation to the benchmark’s bounded power-of-two real-input contract, which normalizes the Java API’s complex input and negative-angle sign convention to the shared fixed-point output. The inverse flag and non-power-of-two padded Java inputs are outside the shared contract.

The pinned Java `FFTBluestein.fftBluestein` applies quadratic chirps, computes a linear convolution through `ConvolutionFFT`, multiplies by the output chirp, and divides by n only for inverse mode. This is distinct from the existing radix-2 transform benchmark: it handles arbitrary transform lengths by reducing to a power-of-two convolution. A bounded forward real-input contract is implemented separately.
This C# file defines the node representation and linked-list pointer operations required by FibonacciHeap; it is a supporting data structure component, not an independent algorithm candidate.
