The pinned Python implementation uses randomized Lomuto partitioning with a <= pivot comparison and recursively searches only the side containing the requested one-based order statistic. The benchmark makes the random pivot stream reproducible with xorshift32 and restricts inputs to distinct bounded integers, matching the source documentation’s expected-linear-time assumption.

The pinned Python implementation computes the same minimum subset-sum difference as the Java minimum_sum_partition source for nonnegative values. It is an alias under the bounded shared domain; empty input also returns zero.

The pinned Java, Python, and R sources all compute the minimum cost from the top-left to bottom-right using only right and down moves. Java uses a one-dimensional DP array; Python accumulates the same recurrence in the grid; R's optimized variant returns the minimum total. On the benchmark's bounded nonnegative grid domain, all three match the flattened row-major contract.

The pinned Python source uses a shrinking sliding window to find the shortest contiguous range whose sum reaches the target. Positive values keep that method valid; the contract excludes zero-target and negative-value cases.

The pinned Rust kruskal(Vec<Edge>, num_vertices) sorts edges by ascending usize cost with sort_unstable_by_key, accepts an edge when DSU merge joins two components, and stops after num_vertices-1 edges. It returns Some((total_cost, selected_edges)) only when that many edges were accepted; disconnected graphs return None. It aliases the scalar kruskal benchmark for 1..64 vertices, zero-based in-range endpoints, and nonnegative weights <= 1,000,000, keeping the total within 32-bit range. Equal-cost edges may produce a different selected-edge vector, which is outside the shared total-cost output. The source's zero-vertex capacity expression underflows, so the shared domain requires at least one vertex.

The pinned Python Boruvka source aliases boruvkas_minimum_spanning_tree on connected simple undirected graphs with 2..16 vertices and integer weights 1..100. Adapt its returned MST graph by summing each symmetric edge once; do not call distinct_weight because it changes input weights. Tied weights may select different MST edges with the same total.

The pinned Python source stable-sorts weighted edges and uses disjoint sets. This is a Kruskal alias of the canonical `kruskal` benchmark; returning ordered forest edges and preserving source tie behavior are output and input-profile differences, not a different algorithm.

The pinned Python source scans and sorts weighted edges, then uses disjoint sets. This is a Kruskal alias of the canonical `kruskal` benchmark; its edge-list output and source-specific graph restrictions do not define a different algorithm.

The pinned Python source runs Prim from vertex zero with an indexed heap. This aliases the canonical `prim` benchmark at the algorithm level; edge-list output and heap tie rules are source-profile details.

Despite the filename, the pinned Python `prims_algo` is Dijkstra: it relaxes `dist[node] + edge_weight` in a keyed min-priority queue and returns distance and parent maps. It aliases the distance-only `dijkstra` benchmark on connected simple undirected graphs with bounded nonnegative weights, encoded as reciprocal directed edges; node insertion order fixes the source. Parent-map tie choices are outside the shared benchmark output.

The pinned Python source uses bottom-up dynamic programming to return the minimum number of square terms whose sum is n. It special-cases zero to return 1 even though the DP base is zero; positive inputs minimize 1+dp[n-j*j]. The benchmark bounds n to 0..4096 and maps invalid values to -1. This count is distinct from a perfect-square predicate or a sum of squares.

The pinned Python source initializes a table with n+1, sets table[1]=0, then scans i upward and relaxes i+1, 2*i, and 3*i in that order when in range. The bounded package preserves the exact forward tabulation result.

The pinned Java implementation returns the minimum absolute difference between two subset sums for nonnegative inputs. The bounded contract preserves this minimum-difference objective; the Python minimum_partition implementation has the same contract on the shared domain. This is distinct from equal-partition decision algorithms, which return a boolean.

The pinned Python mincost_tickets validates travel days in 1..365 and exactly three costs, returns 0 for an empty schedule, then memoizes from day 1. It advances through non-travel days and on each travel day minimizes costs plus recursive states at day+1, day+7, and day+30. The benchmark uses unique days and bounded nonnegative costs.

The pinned Java and Python sources both sort the nonnegative request durations in ascending order and sum each duration multiplied by the number of requests behind it. On the benchmark's bounds of at most 64 durations in 0..1000, this equals the shared weighted-sum contract, including empty and singleton inputs returning zero.

The pinned Java MinimumWindowSubstring.minWindow builds target frequencies, expands a right edge, and contracts while all required characters are present; it updates only for a strictly shorter window, preserving the earliest tie. The pinned Python min_window uses the same multiplicity-aware sliding-window behavior. The benchmark restricts strings to ASCII bytes, excludes the Java empty-target edge case, and returns the shortest matching byte slice or empty output. The pinned R file is explicitly excluded from this benchmark: it is interactive, lowercases inputs and output (unlike the case-sensitive Java/Python contract), uses readline/cat/quit, and references an undefined %||% helper.

The pinned C# Distance method validates order>=1 and equal point lengths, then computes the same generalized Minkowski formula as the Python source. The package p=3..6 bounded contract is a shared subdomain; p=1 and p=2 remain covered by their dedicated Manhattan and Euclidean benchmarks.

The pinned Python and C# sources validate positive order and equal point dimensions, then compute (sum(abs(a-b)^p))^(1/p). The package bounds p to 3..6 and coordinates/dimensions so integer intermediates are exact and safe; all workload outputs are exact roots or zero for the exact-comparison runner.

The pinned MATLAB/Octave minone(x) computes sum(x.^2), a sum-of-squares objective distinct from the existing sum_of_squares minimum-square-summands algorithm. The bounded i64_array_scalar adapter accepts vectors of length 1..64 with values in [-1,000,000, 1,000,000] and returns the exact signed-i64 sum; the maximum 64,000,000,000,000 is below 2^53, so it is exact in MATLAB binary64. Matrix column-sum behavior and non-finite inputs are outside the adapter. Nine-language package, workload, oracle, and README are present; D58 package and integration review and root static integration review are CLEAR. No tests, builds, or verifiers were run.

The pinned C miroir(char *s) reverses a writable NUL-terminated string in place, using compte to count bytes before the terminator, and returns the same pointer. Empty strings are unchanged; the function does not allocate or check null/read-only pointers or buffer bounds. The demo reads one whitespace-delimited token into char[20] with unbounded scanf("%s"), so a safe benchmark should call the function with a bounded writable buffer rather than benchmark the interactive main. D58 formally cleared the nine-language package; 99b registered its byte-output runner/verifier integration, with independent integration review pending.

The pinned Python Node.mirror method recursively exchanges each node’s left and right children, mutates the tree, and returns its root. It is semantically equivalent to C LeetCode 226 and aliases the shared invert_binary_tree benchmark.

The pinned Python source exposes focal-length, object-distance, and image-distance rearrangements of the mirror equation. The package preserves each reciprocal-expression order through a mode adapter, bounds finite nonzero inputs, and maps zero inputs or singular denominators to an explicit ABI sentinel.

The pinned Java mirrorMatrix(double[][]) validates that the matrix and every row are nonnull/nonempty and that all rows have equal length, then returns a new matrix with each row reversed. This is a horizontal reflection: row order is preserved, the input is not mutated, and it is not a transpose or vertical flip. Invalid shapes throw IllegalArgumentException; numeric values such as NaN are not filtered. This matrix operation is distinct from the C mirror entry, which reverses a string.

The pinned Python source evaluates Mish as `x * tanh(log(1 + exp(x)))`, applying exponential, addition, logarithm, hyperbolic tangent, then multiplication in that order. The bounded unary contract preserves this direct formula and source rounding.

The pinned Python source uses the same min/max XOR cancellation algorithm as the Rust find_missing_number source. On the shared contract requiring observed endpoints and one missing interior value, it is an alias.

The pinned Elixir mix.exs defines Mix project metadata only: app/version/Elixir requirement, logger as an extra application, and an empty dependency list. It contains no algorithm implementation or executable benchmark workload, so it is excluded from the algorithm inventory.

The pinned Python `mixed_keyword` function uppercases keyword and plaintext, deduplicates keyword characters that occur in the supplied alphabet, prepends them to the remaining alphabet characters, lays that sequence into rows of keyword-width, then maps the original alphabet vertically by columns. Non-alphabet plaintext characters pass through unchanged. The benchmark should use the default A-Z alphabet and require at least one unique valid keyword letter; a keyword with no valid letters gives a zero step in range() and raises. `verbose` only prints the mapping and is outside the returned-string algorithm.

The pinned Julia ML.jl is a namespace aggregator: it imports TheAlgorithms, exports KMeans, and includes the sibling k_means.jl implementation. It contains no additional algorithm; that exact Julia source-specific candidate is `k_means_julia`, so this module filename aliases it.

The pinned Java class runs a simplified multi-level feedback queue over FIFO queues. All processes enter queue 0; one process per nonempty queue is given min(timeQuantum[level], remainingTime), finished processes are printed, and unfinished processes are demoted one level or requeued at the last level. Because levels are scanned in ascending order, a demoted process may run again in the same outer pass. arrivalTime is stored but ignored, priority is incremented but scheduling uses queue index, and no I/O promotion exists. A bounded contract must require levels>0, a quantum for each level with positive quanta, nonnegative bursts, and bounded currentTime; nonpositive quanta or negative burst times can prevent termination. Console output is ancillary to getCurrentTime().

Both pinned C++ files implement offline Mo range-query ordering and answer the number of distinct values in each 1-based inclusive interval. They use block size ceil(sqrt(n)), sort by left-block then increasing right endpoint, maintain a half-open active range with add/remove frequency updates, and store answers back in input order. Inputs must fit the static N=1e6+5 arrays, have nonempty in-range queries, and use values in [0,N); the sources do not validate these assumptions. The two implementations are otherwise algorithmically equivalent; the C-Plus-Plus-1 file relies on transitive headers for sort/ceil/sqrt/scanf. Output is one distinct-count integer per query.
The pinned Go source matches `mobius_function` for positive inputs, including μ(1)=1 and the prime-square test. Its `n <= 1` shortcut differs outside the shared positive domain.

The pinned Java, JavaScript, and Python sources agree on positive inputs: a repeated prime factor returns zero; otherwise parity of distinct prime factors selects ±1, with μ(1)=1. Nonpositive behavior is excluded from the shared contract.

The pinned Go source returns one most-frequent value but leaves tie selection unspecified because it iterates over a map. The pinned Java and PHP sources return all tied modes. All three agree on the unique mode for nonempty integer arrays; the benchmark restricts values to 0..255 and lengths to 1..4096, with empty, tied, and out-of-domain inputs assigned the documented -1 sentinel.

The pinned C helper narrows candidate rows using the middle column and binary-searches one row slice, matching binary_search2d_array. Its driver allocates m row pointers before filling n rows, so this source is safely exercised only on square matrices; width 1 also reaches an unguarded middle-column neighbor access. The alias therefore applies to strictly increasing square matrices with side 3..32, within the existing contract. The printed [row,column] coordinate maps to the benchmark row-major index.

The pinned Lua source uses binary repeated squaring and modular reductions, the same modular exponentiation algorithm as the canonical `modular_exponentiation` benchmark. Its zero-base assertion and numeric bounds are source-contract details.

The pinned JavaScript ModRing exposes modular add, subtract, and multiply after checking an initialized modulus and numeric operands. The benchmark covers those three operations on canonical residues. The divide method is excluded because its implementation returns an extended-Euclidean Bézout coefficient directly, without multiplying by a numerator or validating an invertible denominator.

The pinned JavaScript function uses exponentiation by squaring recursively: exponent zero returns 1, odd exponents recurse on n-1 and multiply by a, and even exponents square the n/2 result. The benchmark bounds base, exponent, and modulus so all Number products remain exact and preserves the source's un-reduced result of 1 for exponent zero.

The pinned C++ sources compute division by multiplying by b^(p-2) modulo prime p, so their intended domain requires an invertible denominator. The Python source uses extended Euclid, orders parameters as divisor then dividend, and supports coprime divisor/modulus pairs. The shared contract uses C++ tuple order and prime moduli; the Python adapter swaps numerator and denominator arguments and matches the same residue on this domain.

The pinned Python and Rust `modular_exponential` implementations use square-and-multiply and match the existing modular_exponentiation benchmark on the restricted domain base >= 0, power >= 1, and modulus >= 2 (all signed-i32). Python normalizes the base with modulo; Rust has additional inverse behavior for negative powers and a modulus-one special case. Those out-of-domain cases are intentionally excluded; the candidate aliases the existing benchmark without adding another set of ports.

The pinned C++, R, C#, and Rust sources implement modular exponentiation with either binary exponentiation or repeated multiplication. The shared contract uses a nonnegative signed-i32 exponent and positive signed-i32 modulus, normalizes negative bases to the mathematical residue, and uses binary exponentiation in the ports.

The Go source computes base^exponent modulo modulus with square-and-multiply after a modulus-based overflow guard. On the bounded nonnegative input domain, it matches the existing modular_exponentiation contract; negative exponents and negative bases are excluded because the source reports errors or preserves negative remainders.

Pinned Go, Lua, and Nim extended-Euclid APIs agree on nonnegative a in 0..1,000,000 and modulus in 2..1,000,000: return the least positive inverse when gcd is one, otherwise map source-specific absence to -1. Modulus 1 is excluded because Go returns zero while Lua/Nim return absent; negative a is excluded because Go can report a negative gcd.

The pinned C++ source normalizes negative a and rejects zero, while the C++-1 standalone exponentiation leaves negative remainders unchanged. The common contract therefore uses positive a in 1..1,000,000, prime m in 2..1,000,000, and excludes a divisible by m so both copies produce the same inverse. Positive multiples are excluded because the sources can return zero for them.

The two pinned C++ imod() function bodies are identical and use the same successive-itr brute-force search. The benchmark restricts x to 1..999 and y to 2..1,000, with gcd(x,y)=1; this makes the search terminate within x-1 iterations and keeps the intermediate numerator within signed 64-bit range.

The pinned C# Compute method obtains the Bézout coefficient of a from ExtendedEuclideanAlgorithm, throws ArithmeticException unless gcd(a,n)=1, and adds n when that coefficient is negative. The benchmark bounds n to 2..1,000,000 and a to [0,n), returns the canonical inverse in [0,n), and maps invalid/non-invertible inputs to -1.

The pinned Solidity contract stores uint256 firstNo and secondNo through public setters; both default to zero. GetModulo() returns firstNo % secondNo, so divisor zero causes a Solidity revert. The bounded shared contract accepts exactly [a,b] with unsigned 32-bit values and 1<=b<=2^32-1, returns a%b in [0,b), and rejects malformed length, negative values, or values above uint32. This is source-faithful on the bounded domain; it is a demonstration wrapper around Solidity's built-in unsigned remainder operator, distinct from modulo_power_of_two. Source contract CLEARed by 80ac against TheAlgorithms/Solidity commit 08cba51fb38e276062b0c9791d7e0ee494ffa903.

The pinned Java source rejects n<=0 and returns x & ((1 << n) - 1) for signed-i32 x and 1<=n<=31. This yields the low n-bit nonnegative residue, including for negative x; Java’s n=31 overflow still gives the same 0x7fffffff mask. The benchmark bounds n below 32 to avoid Java shift-count wraparound and maps invalid inputs to -1. This is distinct from a power-of-two predicate and from modular division.

This source row maps two distinct helpers from the pinned Python molecular_chemistry.py: mass_to_moles preserves binary64 quotient then two-decimal ties-to-even rounding, while moles_to_molecules preserves binary64 multiplication followed by `.4e` formatting and parsing. Four other helpers in the file remain outside these contracts.

Pinned Rust `src/machine_learning/optimization/momentum.rs` at `fed66cb0c74c4a939ec5163648458a8c2b46fd4c` initializes zero velocity and per iteration computes the derivative at the current vector, then updates zipped coordinates in order: `velocity = beta*velocity + gradient`, `x -= learning_rate*velocity`. The benchmark pins the source test derivative `2*x`, learning rate 0.01, beta 0.9, and 100 iterations with a fresh zero velocity each call. `float64_slice_io` bounds inputs to 1..64 finite values in [-1e6,1e6], returns the same-length updated vector, and compares with absolute tolerance 1e-12 and relative tolerance 1e-10. Invalid input returns -1; null/short output returns -2 without writing. Nine-port package, oracle, workload, and README are present; root static integration review is CLEAR. No builds or tests were run.

The pinned Python class is a stateful NumPy momentum-SGD optimizer. Each `param_id` gets an independent zero-initialized velocity; each call computes `v = momentum*v - learning_rate*gradient`, returns `params + v`, and retains `v` for that ID. The benchmark packs an interleaved multi-ID trace, starts a fresh optimizer per case, and returns final parameters followed by final velocities grouped by ID. It narrows the source's broadcasting and dtype behavior to equal-width finite binary64 vectors. Nine local language ports and runner/verifier integration are statically cleared.

The pinned Java MonoAlphabetic.encrypt/decrypt use uppercase substitution and inverse lookup. The benchmark packs [op,len,key26,text] over uppercase ASCII, requires a permutation key and 1..256 text bytes, and returns low 63 bits of FNV-1a-64 over an unsigned little-endian u64 output length followed by transformed bytes; invalid=-1.

The pinned PHP monoAlphabeticCipher maps between a supplied alphabet and key, copies spaces, removes ASCII digits, and preserves letter case. The benchmark requires uppercase A-Z permutations and 0..128 ASCII text bytes; output is low 63 bits of FNV-1a-64 over an unsigned little-endian u64 output length followed by transformed bytes; invalid=-1.

Cleared Python ABI: [op,len,key26,text...], op 0/1, uppercase permutation key, printable ASCII text length 0..128. Preserve case/nonletters and preserve source wrapper effects (`encrypt_message` performs inverse mapping; `decrypt_message` performs key substitution). FNV-1a-64 hashes output length and bytes; low 63 bits returned; invalid=-1.

The pinned Python source geometry/monotone_chain.py at e1a2a8b016001309a73d5fec4818c35cca139795 implements Andrew's monotone-chain convex hull over Point(x,y) NamedTuple values. It sorts and deduplicates via sorted(set(points)), constructs lower and upper chains, and pops whenever cross_product_direction <= 0; thus collinear interior boundary points are removed, and the hull is counter-clockwise. Empty and one-unique-point inputs are returned directly; two points are lexicographically sorted; all-collinear inputs reduce to endpoints. Bounded adapter CLEAR: input [n,x0,y0,...] with n=0..64 and integer coordinates in [-1,000,000,1,000,000], interpreted as exact-valued floats; these bounds keep all coordinate differences/products exactly representable in binary64. Output hull coordinates as LE signed-i32 pairs, return 8*vertex_count bytes; malformed lengths/range => -1, null/short output => -2. This remains distinct from existing convex hull variants that retain collinear points or require at least three points. Source contract CLEARed by 80ac against the pinned TheAlgorithms/Python commit.

The pinned Python is_monotonic returns true when every adjacent pair is nondecreasing or every adjacent pair is nonincreasing; equal values are allowed, and empty/singleton inputs return true through vacuous all(). The bounded benchmark preserves that predicate for arrays of up to 256 full-range signed-i64 values, returning 1/0 and reserving -1 for invalid input.

Cleared ABI: [n,window,values...], n 1..4096, 1<=window<=n, signed-i32 values. Return ordered sliding-window maxima; source removes older equal maxima with >=. FNV-1a-64 hashes signed-i32 results; low 63 bits returned; invalid=-1.
The pinned Fortran/Python routines are stochastic numerical simulations with no source-level deterministic random-stream injection seam.
The pinned dice simulation is stochastic and exposes no deterministic random-stream injection seam.

The pinned Java seeded overload calls `doApproximate`, which validates a nonnull function, a<b, and n>0. For each of floor(n/2) draws it evaluates `u` then `1-u`; an odd final sample consumes one additional draw. The deterministic adapter supplies those uniform draws explicitly, uses a bounded x^2 integrand, and preserves the source draw order and `(b-a)*total/n` return expression. Julia independent-draw sampling is tracked separately.

The pinned Julia function uses global rand() once for each of n independent samples, accumulates f(x), then returns ((b-a)/n)*sum. It has no explicit seed argument. Its separate deterministic adapter supplies n uniform variates directly, preserving one independent sample per draw and the source multiplication order; it is not aliased to Java antithetic pairing.

The pinned R script simulates geometric Brownian stock paths with dt=T/n, n independent standard-normal increments scaled by sqrt(dt), and S(t)=S0*exp((r-sigma^2/2)t+sigma W); each path contains n+1 values. `monte_carlo_option_price` repeatedly simulates a path, takes the terminal European call payoff max(ST-K,0), averages `num_simulations` payoffs and discounts by exp(-rT). It relies on R's global RNG without setting a seed and performs no parameter validation. The script's top-level demo uses fixed sample parameters and 10,000 simulations; `quantmod` is loaded but unused by the formulas.

The pinned Java class is a fixed-time MCTS demonstration over a synthetic tree, not a game-state search. It adds ten root children, repeatedly selects by UCT (unvisited children first; otherwise mean score + 1.41*sqrt(log(parent visits)/child visits)), expands leaves by ten, and simulates a random win with probability 1/6 using a fresh unseeded Random. Backpropagation adds 10 to nodes aligned with the random winner flag; selection runs for 500 ms, then chooses the root child with maximum score and prints diagnostics. It is excluded as non-benchmarkable because output depends on wall-clock duration and unseeded randomness; replacing the timer with fixed iterations or adding a seed changes the pinned source behavior.

The pinned Go package estimates pi from uniformly sampled points in the unit square, returning 4*inside/randomPoints. `MonteCarloPi` uses a time-seeded local RNG; it does not validate zero/negative sample counts (zero yields NaN). The concurrent variant splits n across `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0)` workers, uses one independently time-seeded RNG per worker, and returns an error when n is less than worker count; otherwise it combines counts and divides by n. It is nondeterministic and its worker partition/seed behavior can differ from the serial function.

The pinned Rust moore_voting_2pass source performs Boyer-Moore candidate cancellation followed by a second pass that verifies a strict majority greater than n/2. It returns None for an empty array or when no strict majority exists, matching the canonical benchmark semantics; the benchmark encodes absence as -1.

Despite the pinned filename Moore_voting_algorithm.dart, the Dart function sorts the supplied list and counts adjacent equal values. It returns a value only when the run length exceeds n/2, otherwise -1. The benchmark preserves this strict-majority result on arrays of 2..128 signed 32-bit values; length one is excluded because the source loop never reports it.

The two pinned C++ files implement the same Morris inorder traversal: when a node has a left subtree, temporarily thread its inorder predecessor back to the node, descend left, then print the node and restore the thread when revisiting it. Output is inorder values with a trailing space. The first repository also has a recursive deleteAll helper; the second omits it. Their mains only build the fixed complete tree with values 1..7 and print a demo. The traversal itself is reusable and has O(1) auxiliary space; it is distinct from stack-based and recursive inorder traversal by its temporary-threading behavior.

Inspected the pinned C++ and C++-1 snapshots, JavaScript, PHP, Python, and Rust sources. All provide an encoder for ASCII letters and digits, but they differ on letter case, punctuation, whitespace, dot symbols, unsupported characters, and trailing or word separators. The shared benchmark covers their common alphanumeric encoding: ASCII case-folding, canonical dot/dash Morse, one space between codes, no trailing separator, empty input as empty output, and explicit invalid-input and capacity statuses. The JavaScript candidate additionally supports punctuation and custom symbols; those extensions are outside the common contract.

The pinned Java class exposes independent textToMorse and morseToText algorithms. The encoder uppercases ASCII letters, maps A–Z, preserves its space-splitting and unsupported-character empty-token behavior, and emits word separators; the decoder splits on the exact word delimiter, maps A–Z codes, drops trailing empty split fields as Java String.split does, and emits ? for unknown or empty codes. The two directions have separate contracts and workloads.

Cleared ABI: [op,n,q,target,arr[n],(left,right,index)*q], n/q 1..256/0..256, values and target bounded to ±1,000,000; range-sum or fixed-target frequency queries use source floor(sqrt(n)) Mo blocks, alternating right sort, and original result order. The pinned Java class is a mutable agent-to-task registry, not a scheduler. addAgent keeps the first Agent for each existing name; assignTask silently ignores unknown names and appends tasks, including duplicates, in call order for known agents. getScheduledTasks copies the map entries from a HashMap iteration and exposes each Agent task list; map order is unspecified. The pinned file is an interactive, hard-coded 20x20 four-neighbor grid-search demonstration, with global map/heuristic/weight/time settings and a fixed obstacle row. The pinned Python `MLFQ.multi_level_feedback_queue` performs one round-robin pass for each of the first `number_of_queues - 1` time slices, then finishes remaining processes in FIFO order. It records waiting, turnaround, stop time, and finish order. The benchmark fixes all arrivals at time zero, preserving the source's queue behavior while excluding its unusual nonzero-arrival current-time update. The packed contract bounds queues to 1–4, processes to 0–8, time slices and bursts to 1–16, and output to signed-i32 finish records.

The pinned C file contains two recursive three-way multikey string quicksorts, ssort1 and ssort2, plus unrelated ternary-search-tree routines and a fixed three-string demo. Both partition on the character at the current depth, recurse on lower and higher characters at the same depth, and recurse on equal characters at the next depth until the NUL terminator. ssort1 chooses a random pivot; ssort2 uses insertion sort below 10 items and median-of-three (pseudomedian-of-nine above 30) pivot selection. The sort is non-stable and uses C plain-char ordering; the benchmark restricts strings to ASCII bytes 1..127 and preserves sorted length-prefixed bytes. The reusable sort is distinct from scalar quicksort because it handles string keys character by character.

The pinned Python source implements a stateful one-hidden-layer MLP with ReLU hidden activations, linear outputs, one-hot labels valued at 0.99, per-sample gradient updates, mean-squared loss, accuracy tracking, and per-epoch learning-rate decay. A module-global NumPy generator seeded once at import initializes weights, so repeated model constructions share RNG state. The toy `Dataloader` hard-codes three training rows and one test row, reports output dimension as the number of training labels rather than distinct classes, and its shuffle method is a no-op; `class_weights` is unused. `train()` stores test accuracy/loss histories and prints average accuracy but returns no predictions or trained weights. This is a multilayer model, distinct from the PHP single-layer perceptron classifier.

The pinned Java class implements multinomial Naive Bayes with configurable alpha > 0 (default 1.0). fit requires nonempty features and one label per row, clears prior state, sets feature width from the first row, accumulates per-class feature sums and sample counts, then stores log priors log(classCount/sampleCount) and smoothed log likelihoods log((featureSum+alpha)/(classFeatureTotal+alpha*numFeatures)). Prediction sums the log prior plus sampleCount[j]*logLikelihood[j] and keeps the first class encountered on equal scores; iteration order comes from HashMap, so ties are not a portable result contract. The batch overload applies the same prediction to each sample. The source documents nonnegative counts but does not validate them or rectangular rows; a bounded port should require rectangular nonempty training rows, positive feature width, finite nonnegative counts, matching prediction width, and unique winning scores. This is distinct from the existing Gaussian Naive Bayes benchmark.

The pinned MATLAB-Octave algorithms/Divisibility_of_integers/multiple.m returns whether mod(x,m)==0. Its source permits zero and negative operands and treats mod(0,0)==0, but the alias is restricted to the existing is_divisible contract's domain: dividend 0..1,000,000,000 and divisor 1..1,000,000,000.

The pinned R file is a short usage fragment, not a callable implementation: it refers to a placeholder data-frame name and four predictor objects, invokes lm directly, then shows a predict call without defining inputs, a function, or a returned result. The pinned MATLAB-Octave Project Euler helper returns its input n when n is divisible by 3 or 5 and zero otherwise. It is a one-term filter, not the Problem 1 sum; its bounded benchmark accepts 0..1,000,000,000 and returns -1 outside that domain.

The pinned Python mux(input0,input1,select) validates each value with Python equality membership in (0,1), then returns input1 when select is truthy and input0 otherwise. Python bool and 0.0/1.0 therefore pass source validation, but the shared benchmark intentionally restricts all three fields to exact integer bits 0/1 to avoid representation ambiguity. The bounded i64_array_scalar contract requires exactly [input0,input1,select], returns the selected 0/1 bit, and returns -1 for invalid framing or values. This is a distinct 2-to-1 Boolean multiplexer; the source contract is CLEARed at TheAlgorithms/Python commit e1a2a8b016001309a73d5fec4818c35cca139795.

candidates.review_notes: The pinned Jupyter notebook uses sklearn-crfsuite and NLTK's CoNLL-2002 corpus to extract features, fit a conditional random field, and evaluate named-entity labels. It depends on an external corpus and ML library/runtime rather than exposing a bounded deterministic algorithm function.
The pinned Python source defines this gate on Boolean integer values 0 and 1. The benchmark contract covers its complete truth table and uses the shared portable scalar ABI.

The pinned Python source enumerates the exclusive range below limit and memoizes each decimal digit power. The benchmark preserves the ascending result list, includes zero for positive limits, and caps the limit at 100000 so the returned 8-byte big-endian values fit the shared output-buffer ABI.

The pinned C# checker counts decimal digits, sums each digit raised to that count, then compares with the input. Zero returns true because both loops are skipped; negative values return false, including INT32_MIN. The benchmark preserves these behaviors within its bounded int32 domain; it is distinct from the enumeration benchmark `narcissistic_number`.

The pinned Python source retrieves NASA APOD/archive API responses; its save path downloads and writes an image file. It depends on external API data and may perform filesystem side effects, so it is excluded from deterministic algorithm benchmarking.

The pinned C# source is an infinite lazy generator beginning at BigInteger 1 and incrementing after each yield. The benchmark maps zero-based index n to n+1, restricts valid indices to 0..INT64_MAX-1 so the result fits i64, and reserves -1 for invalid indices. Indexed ports are O(1) while advancing the source generator is O(n); README documents this cost difference.

The pinned Python source splits digit runs, lowercases text chunks, and relies on Python tuple-key sorting. The bounded benchmark restricts inputs to empty strings or ASCII letter prefixes with optional numeric suffixes, where the shared key preserves the pinned natural-order behavior; equal keys remain stable.

The pinned C source is a terminal Battleship game: it prompts two players to place ships and take alternating shots, renders the board, and terminates based on sunk fleets. Its interactive game loop and user-controlled state have no standalone deterministic algorithm contract suitable for this benchmark harness.

The pinned Python source evaluates the falling product and divides by the factorial of the choose argument. The bounded contract accepts finite fractional totals and exact integer-valued choose inputs, preserving source operation order; this is distinct from integer binomial coefficient packages.

The pinned C++ source precomputes factorials modulo p and uses an extended-Euclid modular inverse for nCr. The package preserves the source’s -1 result when the denominator is not invertible and uses the signed-i64 minimum sentinel for malformed inputs.

The pinned Dart `nearestNeighbourSearch` starts at node 0, repeatedly takes the minimum outgoing edge to an unvisited node, and returns the visitation order. The bounded contract uses integer weights and node-index insertion order to make the source's first-minimum tie behavior deterministic across ports.

The pinned Python KD-tree search evaluates squared Euclidean distance, searches the side selected by query-coordinate <= node-coordinate first, and explores the far side only when squared split distance is strictly below the best distance. It updates the nearest node only for strictly smaller distance and reports nodes visited; the benchmark preserves these tie and pruning rules on validated bounded trees.

The pinned Java source searches a BST for the least key strictly greater than the query and returns 0 when no such key exists. This is an alias of ceil_in_binary_search_tree on the restricted domain where the query is absent and a strict successor exists, so equality and the source zero sentinel cannot affect results.

The pinned Java routine computes the optimal global alignment score using match, mismatch, and linear gap scores. The bounded contract returns the score only and uses a rolling row for the same recurrence.

The pinned Python source evaluates base -2 binary digits as signed positional values. The cross-language contract accepts a most-significant-first bit array of up to 63 digits, ensuring every possible prefix and final value fits signed 64-bit.

The pinned C# source is a lazy BigInteger generator yielding -1,-2,-3,...; zero-based index n maps to -n-1. The benchmark supports every nonnegative i64 index through INT64_MAX, where the result is INT64_MIN, and uses 0 as an invalid sentinel that cannot collide with a term. Indexed ports are O(1), while advancing the source generator is O(n); README documents this cost difference.

The pinned Rust function computes the mean binary negative log-likelihood for paired values, validating equal lengths, nonempty vectors, and values in [0, 1]. The benchmark uses equal-length fixed-point vectors and excludes predicted endpoints because the source formula produces non-finite values there.

The pinned PHP function squares the input, sums the decimal digits of the square, and compares that sum with the input. The shared contract preserves the predicate on nonnegative inputs whose square fits signed 64-bit arithmetic and returns false for negative inputs.
The pinned Python function uses the same three bracket pairs, stack nesting, empty-string behavior, and ignored non-bracket characters as the existing balanced_parentheses benchmark.

The pinned Go implementation uses a stack for the same bracket pairs. On inputs containing only bracket bytes it has the same balanced/unbalanced result as the existing balanced_parentheses benchmark; its handling of other bytes differs, so the alias applies to the target's bracket-only domain.

The pinned Python optimizer initializes velocity to zero for each call and persists it across updates. Each step computes velocity = momentum * previous_velocity - learning_rate * gradient, then updates parameters with params - momentum * previous_velocity + (1 + momentum) * velocity. The bounded contract represents rates and values as thousandths, limits width and steps to eight, and compares the final parameter vector as little-endian binary64.

The pinned Jupyter notebook requests live Netflix pages, parses site-specific HTML with BeautifulSoup, prompts the user to select a category, and prints scraped movie lists. Its output depends on a changing external website and interactive choice, so it is not a deterministic algorithm benchmark.

The pinned C++ and C++-Plus-Plus-1 sources define a multilayer perceptron with matrix-vector forward prediction, sigmoid activation supported at each layer, and no bias terms. Network construction initializes weights randomly, while the source also supports loading explicit saved weights and running single_predict. The shared contract benchmarks the deterministic loaded-model inference path for one hidden layer, sigmoid activations, supplied bounded weights, and bounded input; training, CSV loading, and random initialization are excluded from the measured operation.

The pinned TensorFlow notebook downloads and trains on MNIST through the legacy TensorFlow tutorial loader. Its output depends on external dataset acquisition, neural-network training, and runtime state, so it is not a bounded deterministic benchmark function.

The pinned PHP class exposes a deterministic prediction API using feature-major inputs, caller-supplied weights and bias, sigmoid activation, and a strict output > 0.5 decision. Its separate training routine initializes weights with mt_rand, so the shared benchmark covers predict/inference only and supplies bounded fixed-point parameters directly. Because sigmoid is strictly increasing with sigmoid(0)=0.5, the exact decision reduces to a weighted-sum sign check.

The pinned Java source validates nonempty equal-length point arrays with unique x-coordinates, copies y values into a work vector, and evaluates the standard in-place Neville recurrence at the target. The bounded benchmark preserves that recurrence and update order with integer-valued coordinates and ordinates.

The pinned Python recurrence initializes the first column with y values but indexes x_points[j-i+1], omitting x_points[0]. For two points it returns y[1] unchanged; larger inputs interpolate only a suffix. This is an indexing defect rather than the stated Neville interpolation algorithm.

The pinned Java method compares a recurrence term with an expected signed int; despite its name it does not test primality. Its recurrence has a(0)=a(1)=1 and a(n)=2a(n-1)+a(n-2), but the array write to a[1] makes n=0 invalid. The benchmark preserves valid comparisons for n=1..25, maps invalid inputs to -1, and caps the result at signed 32-bit.

The pinned MATLAB source takes f, df, initial x, and residual tolerance, then iterates x -= f(x)/df(x) until |f(x)| is within tolerance. On the shared newton_raphson domain, use f(x)=x²-radicand, df(x)=2x, the positive start, and tolerance 1e-10; this is the same positive-root Newton iteration within the existing output tolerance.

The pinned Jupyter notebook's `tsum(t, i-1)` indexing yields a first-difference coefficient of 1 and a second-difference coefficient of t, instead of t and t(t-1). The forward interpolation polynomial is therefore evaluated with shifted coefficients and is incorrect for general inputs. Excluded as an invalid implementation of its named algorithm.

The pinned Python implementation builds forward differences for equally spaced x samples and evaluates the Newton forward polynomial. Under the shared Neville contract's bounded integer-valued coordinates, when x nodes are equally spaced, both compute the same interpolating polynomial; this alias is restricted to that node domain.

The pinned Dart source takes a caller function, initial value, iteration count, and centered-difference step. On the shared newton_raphson domain, supply f(x)=x²-radicand, initialValue=start_quarters/4, h=1e-6, and 8 iterations; this follows the normalized recurrence and returns the same positive root within the existing tolerance.

The pinned Python source accepts an arbitrary function and estimates its derivative by a centered finite difference; it stops on residual tolerance and raises on derivative failure or iteration exhaustion. The pinned R source accepts f and fprime and stops on step size; the pinned Rust source accepts f and fprime and runs a caller-selected fixed number of updates. These APIs and stopping rules differ from the fixed cubic newton_raphson_method benchmark and from integer newton_square_root; retain this as a distinct benchmark candidate.

The pinned C++ and C++-1 implementations define f(x)=x^3-4x-9 and f'(x)=3x^2-4, update z=c-f(c)/f'(c), then stop when the saved |f(c)| is below 1e-10. The benchmark follows this fixed-cubic contract with a deterministic bounded initial guess and update limit. The R file with the same normalized filename is a generic f/f' API with a step-size stopping rule and is tracked separately under `newton_raphson`.

The pinned C source hardcodes complex f(z)=z²−3 and f′(z)=2z, starts from a random complex guess, and stops when correction magnitude is at most 1e−10. The pinned Zig source implements generic binary32 Newton updates and stops on a caller-configurable iteration cap or residual epsilon. Neither is equivalent to the fixed cubic newton_raphson_method nor integer newton_square_root; retain this as a distinct benchmark candidate with a deterministic real-input workload.

The pinned C# source uses integer Newton iteration: seed from a power of two near sqrt(n), update `root=(root+n/root)/2`, and stop when root^2<=n<=root^2+2*root, returning floor(sqrt(n)). The contract bounds n to 0..2^62-1. This is a distinct Newton method from `square_root_binary_search` and from floating-point `square_root`, which returns an approximate real value.

The pinned Python function requires exactly one zero among force, mass_1, mass_2, and distance, rejects negative values, and solves the corresponding Newtonian gravitation equation with G=6.6743e-11. The benchmark encodes the missing parameter with a selector, bounds the three supplied values to positive integers 1..1000, and preserves the source formula order for each of the four outputs.

The pinned Python function returns mass * acceleration without positivity checks; it catches exceptions and returns -0.0, but the bounded numeric ABI inputs cannot trigger that fallback. The benchmark preserves signed products on an integral domain bounded to -1,000..1,000.

The pinned C#, Java, Python, and Ruby sources compute each element's next strictly greater value to its right. On the shared positive-value domain, their no-successor sentinels normalize to the canonical `next_greater_nodes` output of zero.

The pinned C++ implementation isolates the rightmost set bit c=x&-x, forms r=x+c, and returns r | (((x^r)/c)>>2). The package preserves that operation over 1..2^30-1, keeping all valid results within positive signed i32. Inputs outside this shared domain return -1; C++ returns zero for x=0 and Java divides by zero, so the benchmark explicitly normalizes that edge.

The pinned Java method uses c=n&-n, r=n+c, and (((r^n)>>2)/c)|r, equivalent to the C++ formula on the shared domain 1..2^30-1. That bound avoids signed-int overflow and keeps results positive. At zero C++ returns zero while Java divides by zero; the shared contract normalizes invalid inputs to -1.

The pinned Go implementation finds the rightmost ascent, swaps its pivot with the rightmost strictly greater successor, then reverses the suffix; when no ascent exists it reverses the whole sequence. All ports preserve the source ordering for duplicates, empty and singleton inputs, and descending wraparound.

The pinned JavaScript and Python sources agree on positive inputs in the benchmark range 1..2^30: return an exact power unchanged, otherwise return the least power of two above it. The benchmark narrows the domain to avoid JavaScript signed-32-bit shift coercions outside the range and maps zero/negative values to -1; Python raises for n<=0 while JavaScript returns 1. This is a ceiling operation, distinct from `find_previous_power_of_two` and the `power_of_two` predicate.

The pinned Python source finds the smallest prime strictly greater than its integer input, including 2 for negative values and zero. It tests primality by trial division, first handling values below two and even values, then checking 6k±1 divisors. The local scalar contract bounds inputs to -4096..4096 and returns -1 outside that range so all target languages have a bounded signed 64-bit workload. The C# PrimeNumber.NextPrime method has the same strictly-greater result when its optional factor is 1 and descending mode is false; those are the benchmark defaults.
Despite its name, the pinned Java method returns the nearest strictly smaller previous element for each input, or -1 when none exists. The output is a little-endian signed-i64 vector.

The pinned Python function returns all fixed-width substrings from left to right, including repeats. The benchmark uses printable ASCII strings and newline-delimited byte output to represent the returned list.
The pinned Python function implements the NIMPLY truth table, returning 1 only for inputs (1, 0). A dedicated bounded Boolean-pair contract and nine target-language ports are provided.

This normalized filename collides across helper types for linked lists, trees, A*, disjoint sets, and development utilities; there is no standalone algorithm or unified node contract. The algorithm-bearing files remain tracked under their own candidate IDs. Excluded as a non-benchmarkable filename catch-all.

The pinned JavaScript Graph.nodeNeighbors scans its undirected edge list in insertion order, adds the opposite endpoint when the queried node is incident, and uses a Set so each neighbor appears once in first-encounter order. The bounded contract uses integer node IDs and retains self-loop behavior.

The pinned Java linked-node stack exposes push, pop, peek, isEmpty, and size with ordinary LIFO behavior. It aliases the shared stack operation-trace contract for valid traces; the benchmark represents the same operations with bounded storage and does not compare the backing-node allocation strategy.
The pinned C# source only declares the NodeState enum values Unconsidered, Open, and Closed; it contains no algorithm or callable operation to benchmark.

The pinned Java implementation runs ready processes by ascending numeric priority and breaks priority ties by earlier arrival. If the ready queue is empty, time advances to the next arrival; a selected process runs to completion. The pinned C filename match does not implement priority scheduling: its completion-time calculator processes linked-list order and ignores the priority field. The bounded contract follows Java and restricts priorities to unique values to avoid PriorityQueue behavior for fully equal comparators.

The pinned Python source repeatedly chooses the ready process with the smallest remaining burst; strict-less comparisons preserve input order on ties, and it reports waiting/turnaround times. On the restricted domain where all arrivals are 0, it matches mode 1 (non-preemptive SJF) of cpuschedulingalgorithms, including stable ties.

The pinned C++ source orders ready jobs by burst time and arrival time, then schedules non-preemptively. Restricting all arrivals to 0 and burst times to distinct positive values removes its unspecified priority-queue tie case and matches mode 1 (non-preemptive SJF) of cpuschedulingalgorithms.

The candidate contains two different generic priority-queue APIs. C# PriorityQueue<T> is a list-backed binary heap over IComparable<T>; it is a min-heap by default and supports a descending/max-heap flag, capacity and collection constructors, Enqueue/Dequeue/Peek/Clear, Count, and GetData. Empty Peek and Dequeue throw InvalidOperationException; GetData exposes the mutable backing list, so callers can break heap order. Equal-priority order is not promised. Dart PriorityQueue<T> stores QueueItem<T> in an ascending sorted List: enqueue inserts before the first strictly greater priority (FIFO for equal priorities), while dequeue removes index 0; both enqueue and dequeue are O(n). Empty dequeue/front/end return null. Its main function is a test/demo. These implementations differ in ordering direction, tie guarantees, complexity, and empty behavior; do not alias them to each other or to the existing list-based/linked-list queues without a narrower shared ADT contract.

The pinned Java source computes single-source shortest paths in directed graphs whose edge weights are 0 or 1, using a deque and strict distance relaxation: zero-weight neighbors go to the front and one-weight neighbors to the back. Unreachable vertices retain Integer.MAX_VALUE; the benchmark encodes those as 255 and finite distances as bytes. This is distinct from unweighted BFS and general-weight Dijkstra.
The pinned JavaScript routine uses the 0/1 include-or-exclude recurrence with memoization and returns the maximum value, matching the canonical optimization result on the shared bounded input domain.

The pinned Kotlin source fills a bottom-up 0/1 knapsack table with the same item/capacity recurrence as the canonical tabulation candidate. This filename is retained as an alias to share one workload and contract.

The pinned C# source is an infinite lazy ISequence that yields BigInteger 0 forever. The benchmark indexes it from zero and returns 0 for every nonnegative i64 input, using -1 only for negative indices. The indexed ports run in O(1), while advancing the source generator to index n takes O(n); README documents that this preserves sequence values rather than generator iteration cost.
The pinned F-Sharp and JavaScript sources compute the raw Z-array with z[0] = 0, matching the canonical contract.

The pinned Java ZigZagPattern.encode emits source characters by row using cycleLength = 2 * rows - 2 and adds the interior diagonal index. It matches candidate 6 and its zigzag_conversion contract on bounded ASCII inputs; rows below 2 and text shorter than the row count return the input unchanged.

The pinned Java source performs breadth-first traversal with the root level left-to-right and alternates direction each level. It returns values grouped by level; the shared contract flattens the same visitation order as zigzag order code 6.

The pinned MATLAB zoomimg.m demo uses a fixed 1.5x factor, rounds each one-based output coordinate divided by that factor to select an input sample, and assigns the sample without smoothing. The benchmark extracts this spatial loop as a bounded grayscale matrix contract and excludes the fixed image-file loading and figure display. The integer coordinate formula matches the source over the declared dimensions. All nine portable ports passed 273 oracle inputs each and recorded 9 workload cases.
